title: Association Between Plasma N-Terminal Tau, Cognitive Decline, and Neurodegeneration in the ADNI Cohort.
abstract:
Blood-based biomarkers offer a cost-effective, minimally invasive alternative to neuroimaging and CSF biomarkers. Newly developed fluid biomarkers, including the N-terminal tau fragment (NT1), show promise for identifying individuals at risk for Alzheimer disease (AD) and for monitoring disease progression. Here, we determine whether NT1 levels are associated with key clinical and biomarker measures in a large, well-characterized cohort.
Participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort with available plasma NT1, β-amyloid (Aβ)-PET, MRI, and clinical measures (Clinical Dementia Rating) were included in this observational study. NT1 was measured using the Quanterix Simoa HD-X platform. PET, MRI, clinical, and other plasma measures were obtained using established ADNI procedures. A subset also had NULISA-based plasma measures of amyloid and tau and tau-PET assessed. Linear regression and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between NT1 and clinical or biomarker measures, adjusting for relevant covariates. Multivariable-adjusted Cox regression was performed to evaluate the association between baseline NT1 levels and risk of clinically diagnosed mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or AD. Mediation analysis was conducted to examine whether hippocampal atrophy mediates the relationship between NT1 and memory decline. Spearman correlations were used to examine continuous relationships between plasma NT1 and continuous fluid and neuroimaging markers.
A total of 755 participants (mean age: 72.9 [7.0], female: 375 [50%]) were included in the study. Plasma NT1 levels were elevated in MCI/AD individuals (BMCI/AD [SE] = 0.09 [0.022], p = 1.98 × 10-4) and were cross-sectionally associated with worse memory performance (B [SE] = -0.25 [0.09], p = 0.005). Aβ moderated the association between elevated NT1 and greater cognitive decline across multiple domains (memory: B [SE] = -0.17 [0.074], p = 0.022; executive function: B [SE] = -0.24 [0.082], p = 0.004; language: B [SE] = -0.21 [0.075], p = 0.006). NT1 levels were negatively associated with hippocampal volume (B [SE] = -264.49 [125.99], p = 0.036) and predicted longitudinal atrophy (B [SE] = -42.00 [16.90], p = 0.013). Accelerated hippocampal atrophy largely mediated the association between higher baseline NT1 level and greater memory decline (B [95% CI]indirect effect = -0.082 [-0.135 to -0.03], p = 0.003, B [95% CI]proportion mediated = 70.1% [32.6%-155.3%], p = 0.004). Higher NT1 levels were associated with higher levels of plasma biomarkers, including NULISA-based brain-derived (BD) plasma pTau (BD-pTau181, BD-pTau217, BD-pTau231: p's < 5.01 × 10-6) and Simoa-Based pTau181 (p < 4.51 × 10-15) and neurofilament light chain (p < 5.34 × 10-7).
Plasma NT1 may be useful in assessing amyloid-dependent cognitive decline and neurodegeneration.

title: Brain Stimulation as a Treatment for Apathy: A Scoping Review of Effects and Safety.
abstract:
Apathy is a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by impairment of goal-directed behavior, cognition, and emotional responsiveness. In this scoping review, the authors evaluated the literature on brain stimulation for the treatment of patients with apathy across diagnostic categories and provide recommendations to guide future research and practice.
The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, and PsycInfo for studies involving brain stimulation for apathy as a primary or secondary outcome.
From 1,209 records, 52 studies evaluating brain stimulation were included; of these, 10 systematic reviews or meta-analyses were synthesized separately. Modalities included repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS; N=26), deep brain stimulation (DBS; N=7), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS; N=6), electroconvulsive therapy (N=1), transcranial alternating current stimulation (N=1), and transcranial pulsating electromagnetic field therapy (N=1). Populations included patients with schizophrenia (N=477), Parkinson's disease (PD; N=289), depression (N=288), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) (N=210), Huntington's disease (N=42), PD with MCI (N=28), traumatic brain injury (N=28), stroke (N=14), COVID-19 (N=12), and dementia with Lewy bodies (N=6) (total N=1,366). rTMS improved apathy measures, most consistently in AD, with positive trends in depression, MCI, stroke, and schizophrenia. tDCS showed variable effects, with some benefits for schizophrenia. DBS showed mixed results, varying with stimulation location. Observed adverse events were mild and modality specific.
Investigations into brain stimulation as a treatment for apathy show some promise. Conclusions were limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous study designs, and variable outcome measures. Randomized trials with common validated apathy instruments, standardized stimulation parameters, and harmonized diagnostic measures may help advance the field.

title: Plasma p-tau181, Aβ1-42, and GFAP across Alzheimer's disease, mixed-type Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, anxiety disorders, and depressive disorders.
abstract:
Blood-based biomarkers including phosphorylated tau181 (p-tau181), amyloid β1-42 (Aβ1-42), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) have been widely investigated for Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection. However, their utility for discriminating neurodegenerative cognitive impairment from anxiety and depressive disorders remains poorly established.
To compare plasma p-tau181, Aβ1-42, and GFAP concentrations across clinically-defined patient groups with AD, mixed-type Alzheimer's disease (MAD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), anxiety disorders (ANX), and depressive disorders (DEP), and to explore their discriminative performance within this cohort.
We recruited 287 participants: AD (n = 80), MAD (n = 41), MCI (n = 54), ANX (n = 53), and DEP (n = 59). Plasma concentrations of p-tau181, Aβ1-42 and GFAP were quantitatively measured using magnetic microparticle chemiluminescence immunoassay. We evaluated inter-group biomarker differences as well as associations between biomarker levels and cognitive performance.
Plasma p-tau181, Aβ1-42, and GFAP concentrations differed significantly across the five diagnostic groups. In the pooled cohort, all three biomarkers showed inverse associations with MMSE scores, although within-group correlations were weaker and inconsistently significant across diagnostic subgroups. ROC analyses showed that p-tau181 and GFAP had numerically higher AUC values than Aβ1-42 in several pairwise comparisons involving AD or MAD and other clinical groups.
Plasma p-tau181, Aβ1-42, and GFAP showed distinct concentration profiles across the clinically-defined diagnostic groups in this exploratory cross-sectional cohort. GFAP and p-tau181 showed moderate-to-good discriminative performance in several pairwise comparisons involving AD or MAD, whereas Aβ1-42 showed comparatively lower standalone discriminative performance.

title: Blood-Based Biomarkers as Predictors of All-Cause Dementia: A 13-Year Follow-Up in the Whitehall II Cohort Study.
abstract:
Blood-based biomarkers are strongly correlated with amyloid positivity in research settings, but their long-term performance in heterogeneous populations remains unclear. Our aim was to determine their long-term prediction accuracy for incident all-cause dementia on their own and when used alongside known risk factors in community-dwelling older adults.
This was a retrospective study based on the UK Whitehall II longitudinal, population-based cohort study established in 1985 among civil servants that includes a clinical examination every 4-5 years. Blood samples stored at the 2013-2013 wave were assayed in 2024 for measures of amyloid-beta (Aβ) 42 and 40, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light (NfL), and phosphorylated tau protein 217 (p-tau217). Incident all-cause dementia, from 2012 to 2013 to 2025, was ascertained from linked medical records, and Cox regression was used to examine associations of biomarkers with dementia, followed by estimation of prediction statistics.
Of the 5,225 (27.2% female) participants (mean age in 2012-2013, 69.4 ± 5.7 years), 516 (30.0% female) had a dementia diagnosis over a 12.2-year median follow-up. Participants with values in the worst quartile of amyloid-beta 42 (Aβ42)/40 ratio (hazard ratio [HR] 1.88; 95% CI 1.57-2.24), p-tau217 (HR 3.74; 95% CI 3.12-4.50), NfL (HR 1.88; 95% CI 1.56-2.28), and GFAP (HR 2.25; 95% CI 1.87-2.72) had higher risk of dementia. The C-index for predicting dementia was highest for p-tau217 (0.693; 95% CI 0.672-0.714), lowest for Aβ42/40 ratio (0.587; 95% CI 0.566-0.608), and was 0.760 (0.738, 0.781) for all biomarkers together. Sensitivity (between 41.7% and 59.5%) and positive predictive value (between 16.4% and 23.5%) of all biomarkers were modest, but specificity (between 76.8% and 78.8%) and negative predictive value (92.3%-94.7%) were good. A second approach to prediction modeling showed a model containing sociodemographic, behavioral, and health-related risk factors to have a C-index of 0.765 (95% CI 0.746-0.785); adding all biomarkers to this model led to a C-index of 0.813 (95% CI 0.795-0.830).
The long-term predictive ability of blood-based biomarkers for incident dementia in community-dwelling older adults was modest due to poor sensitivity and similar to that of a model containing known risk factors.

title: Modifications to cognitive behavioural therapies for depression and anxiety in adults with neurological disorders: A qualitative analysis of intervention protocols.
abstract: Cognitive and Behavioural-based Therapies (CBT) can effectively manage symptoms of depression and anxiety. However, adults with neurological disorders (NDs) often face cognitive, physical, and social challenges that make it difficult to engage with traditional forms of these treatments. To address this, CBT protocols have been modified to better suit the needs of this population. This study analysed 41 randomized controlled trials with modified CBT-based protocols for treating symptoms of depression and/or anxiety in adults with a ND. It spanned 10 different NDs : stroke, epilepsy, migraine, Parkinson's disease, acquired brain injury, multiple sclerosis, and dementia. Content analysis identified seven main categories of modification. These were: (i) neurologically tailored information and skills; (ii) facilitation of learning and retention of information; (iii) cognitive compensatory strategies; (iv) tailoring intervention to individual needs; (v) multi-modal aids of delivery; (vi) caregiver involvement or training; (vii) flexibility of session delivery. These categories were broadly grouped into three main principles of modification: (1) content adaptation, (2) delivery enhancement and (3) caregiver involvement. These findings support the clinical implementation of CBT for adults with NDs and may guide best practices for managing common mental health difficulties in this population.

title: Diabetes mellitus accelerates preclinical Alzheimer's disease progression by amplifying the amyloid-to-tau pathway and attenuating brain-cognition resilience.
abstract: BackgroundDiabetes mellitus (DM) is a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its stage-dependent effects on the ATN framework remain unclear.ObjectiveTo determine whether DM differentially affects clinical progression from cognitively normal (CN) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus MCI to AD, how DM modulates the ATN cascade, and the optimal follow-up for detecting structural-cognitive changes.MethodsWe analyzed longitudinal data from 1638 ADNI participants (765 CN, 71 with DM; 873 MCI, 91 with DM). Clinical progression was assessed by Cox regression. Annualized slopes of ATN biomarkers and cognition were estimated. Moderation analyses tested DM × predictor interactions on A→T (amyloid→tau) and N→C (neurodegeneration→cognition) pathways with FDR correction. Piecewise linear mixed models identified the optimal knot for structural-cognitive coupling.ResultsDM increased CN-to-MCI risk (adjusted HR = 1.73, p = 0.028) but not MCI-to-AD progression (adjusted HR = 1.10, p = 0.574). In CN, DM amplified amyloid-driven tau accumulation in entorhinal cortex (A→T interaction β = 0.77, FDR p = 0.043) and attenuated the protective effect of hippocampal volume on cognition (e.g., hippocampal volume slope × DM on MMSE slope: β = -0.19, FDR p = 0.031). These effects were absent in MCI (all FDR p > 0.05). A 36-month follow-up was the optimal window for detecting robust structural-cognitive coupling in the CN cohort, independent of DM status.ConclusionsDiabetes accelerates preclinical AD by amplifying A→T and eroding structural-cognitive resilience, but does not hasten progression from established MCI to AD. A minimum 36-month observation period is recommended for early-phase prevention trials.

title: Neurodegenerative Diseases: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, Classification, Pathophysiology, Clinical Features, Diagnosis, and Therapeutic Strategies.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a growing cause of disability worldwide, particularly as populations age. Although these disorders differ in etiology and clinical presentation, advances in genetics, neuropathology, and biomarker research have identified shared disturbances in protein homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and immune regulation. These processes may contribute to selective neuronal vulnerability and neural circuit dysfunction. These findings are refining disease classification and diagnosis, yet effective disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Disease-specific abnormalities remain essential to clinical interpretation and treatment selection. Existing reviews often focus on individual disorders or isolated mechanisms, leaving the links between shared biology and disease-specific phenotypes insufficiently clear. We synthesize evidence on the epidemiology, risk factors, classification, and pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Friedreich's ataxia, and multiple sclerosis. We compare their clinical manifestations and diagnostic approaches, including the evolving role of biomarkers, and critically assess established and emerging therapies. By distinguishing shared mechanisms from disease-specific abnormalities, we identify key translational gaps and explore how common biological disturbances may lead to distinct clinical trajectories. This cross-disease perspective may inform diagnostic reasoning, treatment development, and future comparative research.

title: The entorhinal cortex atrophy score for diagnostic distinction between phases of the Alzheimer's disease continuum.
abstract:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common type of dementia, causing functional impairment in millions of individuals and accounting for a large amount of healthcare costs. The entorhinal cortex appears to be one of the first brain structures affected by AD in its early stages. The Entorhinal Cortex Atrophy (ERICA) score is a visual atrophy score used by neuroradiologists in clinical practice for the diagnosis of AD.
To analyze the effectiveness of the ERICA score for distinguishing between patients with subjective cognitive decline (SCD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD dementia.
A systematic review of the literature was conducted on the Science Direct, PubMed, Virtual Health Library, and Cochrane databases, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Of 1,413 studies identified, 6 were ultimately included in the present review, comprising 844 participants: 2 retrospective cohort studies and 4 cross-sectional studies. The methodological quality of the studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale. The focus was on the diagnostic performance of the ERICA score in the continuum phases of AD.
The ERICA score had lower sensitivity than the medial temporal lobe atrophy (MTA) score but higher specificity, reinforcing its importance for diagnostic accuracy, especially in contexts of clinical uncertainty. The ERICA score showed reproducibility between examiners similar to or greater than that of the MTA score. There are a few heterogeneous studies in the current literature on the applicability of the ERICA score in clinical practice.
Diagnostic accuracy of the ERICA score is satisfactory in differentiating SCD or MCI from AD dementia.

title: Naturalistic Driving Engineered Trajectories Forecast Future Cognitive Decline.
abstract:
Early population-based screening for Alzheimer's disease remains limited by the scalability and accessibility of conventional biomarker testing. We tested whether passive naturalistic driving changes predict progression from cognitively normal status to sustained mild cognitive impairment.
Season-adjusted monthly driving data from 298 older adults, including 25 progressors, were summarized into within-person trajectory features capturing drift and instability in cornering and destination diversity relative to a six-month baseline. A GEE logistic regression was evaluated under leave-one-out cross-validation with a paired-consecutive flagging rule. Landmark survival analyses at 12 and 24 months assessed prognostic value. Five held-out clinical subgroups (n = 82 evaluable), plasma pTau217, MoCA trajectories, and depression scores provided independent post hoc validation.
The model detected 19/25 progressors (AUC=0.752, 95%CI: 0.627-0.863; 76% sensitivity; 75% specificity) with an 18-month median lead time before sustained CDR conversion. Adding static baseline driving features reduced discrimination (AUC=0.702), supporting that within-person driving change, not absolute level, carries a predictive signal. Driving markers stratified risk at 12 months (HR = 6.02, 95%CI: 2.35-15.41) and 24 months (HR = 13.38, 95%CI: 3.03-59.04). Signals converged or were directionally consistent with higher pTau217 among detected progressors and clinically ambiguous single-endpoint cases, whereas flagged stable participants showed MoCA decline without pTau217 enrichment. Depressive symptoms did not explain the driving signal (Spearman rho=0.05, p=0.53). The sustained conversion rate (12.3/1,000 person-years) matched epidemiological expectations.
Scalable driving-trajectory features can detect preclinical functional decline with clinically meaningful lead time, without demographic, genetic, or cognitive data, and may serve as an objective neurobehavioral screening tool.

title: Associations Between Biomarkers of Alzheimer's Disease and Sleep in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults.
abstract:
Sleep disturbances have been implicated as a risk factor for developing Alzheimer's disease (AD), but evidence linking plasma AD biomarkers to sleep in cognitively unimpaired individuals remains limited. The present study examined associations between evening, morning, and overnight changes in plasma AD biomarkers and measures of sleep macro- and microstructure and subjective sleep quality in older adults.
Forty cognitively unimpaired adults aged 55 to 75 years (20 females) without sleep or mental disorders underwent overnight polysomnography. Plasma AD biomarkers p-tau181, p-tau217, t-tau, Aβ42, Aβ40, and Aβ42/40 were assessed in the evening and in the morning and related to sleep macro- and microstructure (sleep spindles, EEG spectral power), and subjective sleep measures by using correlational analyzes.
Higher evening t-tau and p-tau181 were associated with reduced N3 sleep, whereas higher morning t-tau and greater overnight increases in t-tau were related to longer nocturnal wakefulness. Amyloid-β measures showed the most consistent associations with sleep microstructure. Higher Aβ42 and Aβ40 concentrations were associated with shorter duration and lower density of sleep spindles, particularly at frontal sites. Higher evening and morning amyloid-β concentrations were also associated with lower alpha, beta, and spindle-frequency EEG power, mainly during non-rapid eye movement sleep. Tau associations with EEG spectral power were less consistent.
In cognitively unimpaired older adults, plasma AD biomarkers were associated with PSG sleep features, especially amyloid-β markers with sleep microstructure. These exploratory, correlational findings suggest that sleep spindles and spectral power may reflect early AD-related biological processes but require replication in larger cohorts.

title: ADHD symptom positivity and its association with medication adherence and psychiatric burden in adults with epilepsy.
abstract:
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms are increasingly recognized in adults with epilepsy (AwE) and may contribute to psychiatric burden, seizure-related outcomes, and treatment adherence. We therefore investigated the frequency of ADHD symptom positivity and its associations with medication adherence, psychiatric symptoms, seizure burden, and neurophysiological findings.
This cross-sectional study included 100 AwE and 94 healthy controls. ADHD symptoms were assessed using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1). Anxiety and depressive symptoms were evaluated using the Beck Anxiety Inventory and Beck Depression Inventory, respectively. Medication adherence was assessed using the Morisky Medication Adherence Scale (MMAS-8). Participants were classifiedas ASRS-positive or ASRS-negative according to the six-item ASRS Part A screener. Clinical, psychiatric, electroencephalographic, and magnetic resonance imaging findings were compared between groups. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors independently associated with ADHD-symptom-positivity.
ADHD-symptom-positivity was significantly more frequent in AwE than in healthy controls (50.0% vs. 25.5%, p = 0.001). Within the epilepsy cohort, ASRS-positive participants demonstrated lower medication adherence (p = 0.010), higher rates of poor adherence (70.0% vs. 48.0%, p = 0.042), higher anxiety (p = 0.002), and depression scores (p < 0.001). Clinically significant anxiety and depression were also more common among ASRS-positive participants (p = 0.027 and p < 0.001, respectively). In multivariable analysis, depression score was independently associated with ADHD-symptom-positivity (OR = 1.147, 95% CI 1.039-1.267, p = 0.007).
ADHD-symptom-positivity is common in AwE and is associated with poorer medication adherence in the between-group analysis, but this association did not remain statistically significant after multivariable adjustment, while greater psychiatric symptom burden was observed. Routine screening for ADHD-related symptoms may facilitate identification of adults with epilepsy at increased riskfor adverse clinical outcomes and support more comprehensive epilepsy care.

title: The uncinate fasciculus in frontotemporal dementia subtypes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of diffusion-tensor imaging studies.
abstract: BackgroundFrontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a leading cause of early-onset neurodegeneration with selective frontal and temporal lobe degeneration. Despite well-characterized gray and white matter atrophy patterns across FTD subtypes, the extent of degeneration of the uncinate fasciculus (UF) tract has not been systematically quantified across FTD subtypes.ObjectiveTo compare uncinate fasciculus fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, radial diffusivity, and axial diffusivity between frontotemporal dementia subtypes and healthy controls.MethodsWe systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of diffusion tensor imaging studies published between 2011 and October 2025 according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines.ResultsWe systematically reviewed 11 studies and performed a meta-analysis of 540 participants across 10 studies. We found that all FTD subtypes demonstrated significant degeneration of the UF compared to controls. The greatest effect sizes were observed when comparing the left UF between the semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA) and controls (FA: SMD = -2.5396, 95% CI: -3.7914, -1.2878, p < 0.0001; RD: SMD = 2.2414, 95% CI:1.7972, 2.6855, p < 0.0001; AD: SMD = 1.9831, 95% CI: 1.1434, 2.8227, p < 0.0001; MD: SMD = 2.5268, 95% CI: 1.9993, 3.0542, p < 0.0001), while the behavioral variant (bvFTD) showed the largest reduction in right UF fractional anisotropy. Within-group analyses revealed significant left-right asymmetry in svPPA and non-fluent aphasia (nfvPPA), with greater left UF involvement, while bvFTD and controls showed no hemispheric differences.ConclusionsWe highlight the UF as a promising tract for understanding disease mechanisms and developing imaging biomarkers in FTD.

title: Multimodal evidence associated with 20Hz rTMS in AD: neuroaxonal injury reduction, neural oscillatory rebalancing, and multilayer network integration.
abstract: High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been demonstrated to enhance cognitive function in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the neurobiological mechanisms associated with neuroaxonal injury, neural oscillatory dynamics, and large-scale network reorganization remain unclear. In this study, we first conducted a randomized, sham-controlled trial with 16 patients with AD to evaluate the efficacy of DLPFC-targeted rTMS, followed by a single-arm multimodal cohort study of 30 patients to explore potential neurobiological mechanisms through cognitive assessments, blood biomarkers, EEG oscillatory activity, and multiplex brain network analysis. In Stage 1, the sham group showed no significant pre-post changes in MMSE or MoCA scores (MMSE: Z = -0.738, Cohen's r = 0.26; MoCA: Z =-0.853, Cohen's r = 0.30). The active rTMS group showed improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.124, Cohen's r = 0.75) and MoCA (Z = -2.108, Cohen's r = 0.75). In stage 2, rTMS was associated with improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.863, Cohen's r = 0.523) and MoCA (t = -6.137, Cohen's r = 0.752) scores. Biomarker analyses indicated a significant decrease in NfL concentrations (Z=-2.371, Cohen's r=0.484). EEG recordings revealed a decrease in delta power in the left temporal lobe (t=2.158, Cohen's r=0.372) and increases in beta power in the right parietal lobe and gamma power in the temporal lobe (beta: Z=-2.088, Cohen's r=0.381; gamma: Z=-2.129, Cohen's r=0.389). Network analysis showed reduced modularity and enhanced global efficiency across theta, alpha, and beta bands, accompanied by increased degree of overlap in frontal, parietal, and occipital regions. Importantly, MoCA improvement correlated with gamma-band global efficiency (R=0.389, P=0.034) and multilayer clustering coefficients in the left frontal and right occipital regions (R=0.478, P=0.008; R=0.398, P=0.029). Overall, rTMS exposure was associated with cognitive improvements in patients with AD, together with changes in neurodegeneration-related biomarkers and EEG network organization. These findings suggest that cognitive changes following rTMS may be associated with oscillatory modulation and large-scale network remodeling. title: Biomarkers and Prognostic Factors in Multiple System Atrophy: A Protocol for a Three-Year, Multicenter, Prospective, Longitudinal Cohort Study in Japan and South Korea.
abstract:
Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a sporadic, adult-onset neurodegenerative disorder characterized by autonomic failure, Parkinsonism, and cerebellar ataxia. Early diagnosis remains a major unmet need because current clinical criteria often identify the disease only after considerable progression. The recently proposed Movement Disorder Society (MDS) prodromal MSA criteria provide a framework for earlier recognition; however, their specificity is limited. In particular, individuals who initially present isolated parkinsonism or cerebellar ataxia without overt autonomic dysfunction may be overlooked, although some of them eventually progress to MSA. To address this critical gap, this multinational, multicenter study aims to clarify the earliest detectable clinical and biological phases of MSA, identify predictors of disease conversion, and refine prodromal diagnostic criteria within a well-characterized East Asian cohort.
This project will be conducted across multi-centers in Japan and South Korea in two phases. Phase 1 is a retrospective analysis of patients initially suspected but not diagnosed with MSA, who were later confirmed as probable or clinically established MSA, to delineate early clinical, imaging, and autonomic features. Phase 2 is a prospective longitudinal cohort enrolling patients aged 30-80 years classified as mono-system MSA (moMSA), possible prodromal MSA according to MDS criteria, or pure autonomic failure. Participants will undergo standardized clinical, neuroimaging, and biomarker assessments including serum and CSF every six months for up to 36 months to identify predictors of conversion to probable or clinically established MSA.
This protocol represents the first multinational effort in East Asia to establish a longitudinal prodromal MSA cohort. By integrating clinical, neuroimaging (brain MRI), and biomarker data (α-synuclein strain and genetic analysis), the study aim to clarify the earliest detectable phase of MSA, refine prodromal diagnostic criteria, and provide a platform for future disease-modifying trials.

title: Validation of the diagnosis of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: Challenges and lessons learned.
abstract:
Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome (LGS) is a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy characterized by multiple seizure types, cognitive impairment, and distinct electroencephalographic (EEG) findings. However, evolving diagnostic criteria, heterogeneous clinical features, and inconsistent electronic health record (EHR) documentation complicate accurate diagnosis and cohort identification. As part of a Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute-sponsored study developing EHR-based computable phenotypes for LGS, we established a reference standard through retrospective chart review and epileptologist classification.
A multicenter retrospective chart review was conducted across seven pediatric epilepsy centers. Stratified sampling using PCORnet data selected patients based on the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision diagnosis code for LGS or other intractable epilepsy diagnoses between 2016 and 2022. Clinical teams abstracted seizure history, EEG findings, developmental status, and treatment history. Two epileptologists independently reviewed each case as classic LGS, pragmatic LGS, or not LGS. Discordant cases underwent adjudication by a senior epileptologist. Cases with incomplete or unclear data underwent repeat abstraction and review.
Of 997 identified patients, 935 underwent classification after exclusions. Initial epileptologist disagreement occurred in 105 cases (11%, unweighted Cohen kappa = 82%). Following adjudication, 130 cases underwent reabstraction to retrieve additional EEG reports and clinical details. Rereview reclassified 67 cases initially considered "not LGS": 33 classic LGS, 12 pragmatic LGS, and 22 excluded for insufficient data. Key EHR challenges included inconsistent EEG reporting, incomplete seizure type characterization, fragmented documentation of cognitive impairment, unclear age at onset, and variable terminology across institutions and providers. Slow spike-and-wave EEG findings were the most frequently missing diagnostic element.
Validating LGS diagnoses using EHR data is complex and resource intensive. Standardized terminology, structured documentation, and rigorous multicenter validation may improve diagnostic accuracy, research cohort identification, computable phenotype development, and longitudinal care for individuals with LGS. Our results highlight important operational lessons for multicenter rare epilepsy studies and underscore the need for improved diagnosis pathways and longitudinal care systems for those with LGS and their families.

title: The Role of Astrocytes in the Inflammatory Response in Neurodiseases.
abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Implementing the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center Uniform Data Set (v3) within the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study.
abstract:
The Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) was a randomized clinical trial designed to prevent type 2 diabetes (T2D) in adults with prediabetes. The DPP Outcomes Study (DPPOS) is the 30-year follow-up of this cohort, focusing on T2D, prediabetes, and related complications. Cognitive assessments began in 2009 and expanded in 2022 to examine cognitive impairment, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and AD related dementias (ADRD), in the surviving cohort. To support these aims, the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center Uniform Data Set version 3 (NACC-UDSv3), the standardized framework used by Alzheimer's Disease Research Centers, was implemented in DPPOS in 2022 to enable data sharing with NACC. These forms were complemented by cognitive tests administered in DPPOS. We aimed to integrate the NACC-UDSv3 into the existing longitudinal DPPOS framework while maintaining fidelity to its structure and developing automated reports to streamline cognitive outcomes adjudication.
Items from the 16 NACC-UDSv3 data forms were compared with those already collected within DPPOS to integrate overlapping similar items, add missing NACC-UDSv3 items, and create a dataset harmonized with NACC-UDSv3. Forms were adapted for electronic data capture (EDC) using the MIDAS (Multimodal Integrated Data Acquisition System, George Washington University). Automated reports integrated current and prior neuropsychological scores to support adjudications. In the first wave of the DPPOS-AD/ADRD study, 1561 cognitive adjudications were successfully completed using the harmonized DPPOS and NACC-UDSv3 data implemented into MIDAS.
The DPPOS-AD/ADRD project demonstrated that NACC-UDSv3 can be successfully integrated into a long-standing longitudinal cohort not originally designed for AD/ADRD research. The harmonization, electronic capture, and automated adjudication processes may provide a practical framework for other cohorts seeking to incorporate NACC-UDSv3 to align with national AD/ADRD research standards.

title: Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation.
abstract: There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above ~60 Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. Furthermore, we derived an analytical formula for idealized neuron models which can approximately predict the tES sensitivity of different cell types at any given frequency. By characterizing the role of morphology and stimulation frequency in determining tES responses of single cells, this is an important step towards a better understanding of tES at the fundamental level. These results also provide an efficient and accurate method for characterizing and comparing the tES responses of different neural populations across the frequency spectrum, which facilitates optimizing tES for cell-type specific targeting.

title: Sleep Spindles and Slow Oscillations as Potential Biomarkers and Therapeutic Targets in Mild-to-Moderate Alzheimer's Disease.
abstract:
This review critically evaluates evidence on sleep spindles (SP), slow oscillations (SOs), and their coordination in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (AD), focusing on their relationships with cognition, AD biomarkers, and their therapeutic potential.
Longitudinal studies associate greater SP and/or SO activity with better cognition and favourable amyloid and tau profiles after clinical onset. Spindle and SO coupling may index network integrity. Preserved NREM sleep oscillations are associated with lower orexin concentrations and weaker adverse relationships between orexin and cognitive and neuropsychiatric outcomes. Closed-loop acoustic stimulation and slow-oscillatory transcranial direct-current stimulation can modify SO activity, spindle activity, and coupling, although cognitive and biomarker benefits remain uncertain. Spindle-SO activity, including their temporal coupling, are associated with cognition and AD biomarkers across the disease continuum. Closed-loop acoustic and electrical stimulation can modify these oscillations, but biomarker-characterized trials in MCI and AD are needed to determine whether treatment produces durable cognitive and biomarker benefits.

title: Mechanisms of Seizure Generation and SUDEP in Cortical Dysplasia: A Role for Cortical Up and Down States.
abstract: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) remains the primary cause of epilepsy-related mortality, yet the preictal brain dynamics that distinguish fatal from nonfatal seizures are not well understood. Identifying the network mechanisms determining these outcomes is critical for developing SUDEP risk biomarkers. Using a neuron-specific PTEN knockout mouse model of cortical dysplasia-which exhibits spontaneous seizures and SUDEP-like events-we employed long-term video-EEG monitoring to analyze cortical state transitions and network signatures. We found that nonfatal seizures are preceded by a progressive "ramp-up" of cortical up and down states, characterized by alternating neuronal depolarization and hyperpolarization, which appears to facilitate seizure initiation. In sharp contrast, sudden death is preceded by a marked suppression of these state transitions and the emergence of infraslow EEG activity, suggestive of spreading depolarizations. This pattern differed from the sustained spike-wave complexes and preserved state transitions observed during status epilepticus. These physiological differences are mirrored behaviorally: nonfatal events typically feature forelimb clonus and spike-wave discharges, whereas fatal seizures are characterized by kicking, tonic hindlimb extension, and diffuse EEG attenuation. Together, these findings suggest that cortical up and down states support seizure initiation, while their disruption and failure to recover postictally predisposes neocortical networks to spreading depression episodes that very likely propagate to brainstem circuits, ultimately triggering SUDEP. By delineating these divergent peri-ictal signatures, this study identifies candidate neurophysiological markers for SUDEP risk stratification.

title: Pharmacological Activities of Centella asiatica: A Systematic Review of Preclinical and Clinical Evidence on Cardiovascular, Neurological, Antioxidant, and Anti-inflammatory Effects.
abstract: Centella asiatica (L.) (Gotu Kola) is a medicinal herb traditionally used in Asia for cognitive enhancement, wound healing, and systemic disorders. This systematic review appraises preclinical and clinical evidence on its cardiovascular and neurological effects. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov (to June 2026) for studies of whole-plant extracts or bioactive compounds (asiatic acid, asiaticoside, madecassoside, madecassic acid, caffeoylquinic acids) in vitro, in animals, or in humans, excluding dermatological studies, reviews, and articles lacking methods. Sixty-two studies met criteria: 54 preclinical and eight clinical trials, assessed using SYRCLE, an in vitro checklist, and Cochrane RoB 2. Preclinically, C. asiatica modulated ischemia-reperfusion injury, reduced doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity, improved cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's models, and showed antidepressant-like effects, via Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant activation and NF-κB/MAPK anti-inflammatory suppression. Clinical evidence was mixed: Gotu Kola matched or exceeded folic acid for poststroke vascular cognitive impairment, and three trials of a standardized triterpenic fraction (TTFCA) improved microcirculation in venous hypertensive and diabetic microangiopathy; however, a type 2 diabetes trial found no significant effect on glycated hemoglobin, glucose, or LDL cholesterol, a mild cognitive impairment trial found no added benefit over exercise alone, and a Phase 1 safety trial is ongoing. C. asiatica shows preclinical promise as a multitarget cardiovascular and neurological agent, but clinical evidence remains limited and inconsistent, compounded by an 800-fold preclinical dosing range, variable treatment durations, and geographic concentration (47% from one country). Larger, standardized, multiregion trials targeting these outcomes are needed before therapeutic claims are warranted.

title: Mild cognitive impairment in presymptomatic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are clinically and biologically related, and each may be preceded by a prodromal stage of disease. Mild cognitive and behavioural impairment (MCI/MBI) have also been observed in those with clinically manifest ALS. The primary aim of this study was to characterise MCI in presymptomatic ALS.
Criteria for frontotemporal-related MCI (MCI-ft), which require evidence of subthreshold cognitive performance or decline, were adapted from existing frameworks for MCI in prodromal FTD, presymptomatic ALS and clinically manifest ALS. MCI-ft was characterised in 216 Pre-fALS participants (74 C9ORF72, 94 SOD1, 20 other pathogenic variant carriers and 28 non-carriers) with neuropsychological data at 807 study visits. All designations were reviewed by a research neuropsychologist, with consensus discussions as needed.
MCI-ft was observed in 15 (20%) C9ORF72, 12 (13%) SOD1 and 3 (%) of other carriers at one or more study visits, compared to 1 (4%) non-carrier. Most visits with MCI-ft showed impairment affecting both language and executive functioning. Fluctuations in MCI-ft status between assessments were common.
The observed frequency and temporal course of MCI-ft in presymptomatic ALS, using criteria based on subthreshold cognitive performance and decline, expands understanding of this phase of disease. These findings help to inform future research examining the risk of phenoconversion to clinically manifest disease and aid the design of disease prevention trials.

title: Depression in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's disease: Clinical manifestations, biomarker evidence, and predictive implications.
abstract: Depression is one of the earliest and most frequent non-motor symptoms in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's disease (PD), often preceding motor signs by years to decades. This review synthesizes epidemiological, neuroimaging, biomarker, and genetic evidence to clarify whether depression is a risk factor, a direct prodromal manifestation, or both. Meta-analyses consistently show a two-fold increased risk of subsequent PD in individuals with depressive symptoms or major depressive disorder (MDD), with the highest risk occurring within 1-2 years of diagnosis but persisting for up to 25 years. Late-onset depressive syndrome (after age 50-60) is associated with dopaminergic deficits on dopamine transporter imaging in 24-79% of cases, supporting it as a prodromal symptom, whereas early-onset depression may act through shared genetic vulnerability or chronic inflammatory pathways. Neuroimaging in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) reveals that depression correlates with caudate atrophy, frontostriatal white matter disruption, and brainstem monoaminergic dysfunction, but not simply with nigrostriatal denervation. Depression frequently coexists with RBD, autonomic dysfunction, and olfactory impairment, likely reflecting shared brainstem pathology. Genetic forms of PD (GBA1, SNCA, LRRK2, PRKN) show variable depression prevalence, providing mechanistic insights into lysosomal, inflammatory, and proteostatic pathways. Emerging evidence implicates IL-17A, sIL-2R, and α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation as convergent points linking depression and prodromal α-synucleinopathy, with gut-brain axis dysfunction potentially amplifying this process. Current Movement Disorder Society prodromal PD criteria include depression but have limited sensitivity in general populations. No disease-modifying trials have tested whether treating prodromal depression alters phenoconversion risk. We conclude that proximal, late-onset depressive syndrome is a robust prodromal marker, while distant or early-onset depression, including MDD, identifies a chronically elevated risk population. Future studies should integrate multimodal biomarkers and test therapeutic interventions in prodromal cohorts.

title: Shared cortical morphometry and molecular signatures across depression and physical diseases.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly comorbid with physical diseases, suggesting shared neurobiological mechanisms. However, the common structural and molecular substrates underlying this comorbidity remain poorly understood. We analyzed multimodal MRI data from 577 patients (MDD, asthma, fibromyalgia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, type 2 diabetes) and 275 healthy controls, constructed individual morphometric similarity networks (MSN) to identify shared cortical alterations, and applied principal component analysis with multiscale molecular annotation (transcriptomic, cell-type, neurotransmitter, and cognitive mapping) to characterize underlying mechanisms. All patient groups exhibited regional MSN abnormalities. A shared MSN pattern emerged, featuring increased similarity in visual and somatomotor regions and decreased similarity in ventral attention, limbic, and default mode networks, and was replicated in independent cohorts. This pattern was significantly associated with spatial gene expression enriched for synaptic signaling, membrane potential regulation, and neuronal architecture, with predominant expression in excitatory/inhibitory neurons and astrocytes. It further mapped onto specific neurotransmitter systems, with exploratory cognitive decoding suggesting possible relevance to emotion and social cognition. Related genes overlapped with known risk loci for Alzheimer's disease and bipolar disorder. These findings identify a robust across diseases cortical MSN phenotype linked to convergent molecular and neurochemical correlates, offering a framework for studying shared vulnerability and transdiagnostic mechanisms across depression and physical diseases.

title: Effects of cannabidiol (CBD) oral solution in patients undergoing bilateral total knee arthroplasty: a randomized, controlled, parallel, triple blind, pilot study.
abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD) is a non-intoxicating phytocannabinoid with limited clinical evidence of its analgesic and opioid sparing effects. In the United States, the oral cannabidiol solution, Epidiolex®, is FDA-approved for intractable seizures. We conducted an off-label pilot randomized trial to evaluate its perioperative effects in patients undergoing bilateral total knee arthroplasty (BTKA). After IRB-approval and trial registration (NCT04749628), 36 patients were randomized to receive four perioperative doses of placebo (n=12), 400mg (n=12) or 800mg (n=12) oral CBD with standardized anesthesia and multimodal analgesia. The primary outcome was cumulative 72-hour opioid consumption (MME). Secondary outcomes included pain scores, adjunct analgesic use, inflammatory markers (IL-6), sleep, mood (HADS), safety, and pharmacokinetics. Dunnett's test showed no significant differences in 72-hour opioid consumption versus placebo (400mg: 144 vs 209 MME, p=0.10; 800mg: 203.2 vs 209 MME, p=0.98), although post hoc testing demonstrated lower opioid use with 400mg CBD compared with placebo (p=0.04). The 400mg group also had lower pain scores and fewer rescue analgesic requirements, but greater NSAID use. The 800mg group showed no opioid-sparing effect and had greater adverse event burden. CBD groups reported improved subjective sleep domains, while anxiety and depression scores were higher, particularly at 800mg. IL-6 levels were higher in CBD groups. Pharmacokinetic analyses confirmed measurable, dose-dependent exposure with substantial interindividual variability. These pilot data suggest a potential therapeutic signal at moderate dosing but not at higher doses. Larger trials are needed to confirm efficacy and define optimal dosing. PERSPECTIVE: Among BTKA patients, 400mg cannabidiol reduced opioid use and pain while remaining tolerable, whereas higher dosing increased side effects, supporting further evaluation of CBD analgesia.

title: Levetiracetam versus valproate for new-onset or previously treated but inadequately controlled epilepsy in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
abstract:
To compare the efficacy and safety of levetiracetam versus valproate in children with new-onset or previously treated but inadequately controlled epilepsy.
We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library from inception to April 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing levetiracetam versus valproate in children (aged 0-18 years) with new-onset or previously treated but inadequately controlled epilepsy. Outcomes included seizure freedom, exploratory analyses of survival time without seizure and time to first seizure recurrence, change in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels, and adverse events.
Eight RCTs involving 1,000 participants were included. Seizure freedom did not differ significantly between treatments (5 studies, 655 participants; RR = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.83-1.09; P = 0.45; I² = 59.5%; low-certainty evidence). Exploratory time-related outcomes favored valproate but were limited by low-certainty evidence and inadequate handling of censoring. Levetiracetam was associated with lower AST levels, although this did not establish superior hepatic safety, and with fewer overall adverse events and less weight gain.
No significant difference in seizure freedom was detected between levetiracetam and valproate, although the low-certainty finding was sensitive to one trial. Time-related outcomes favored valproate but were exploratory and limited by inadequate handling of censoring. Levetiracetam was associated with fewer overall adverse events and less weight gain, while behavioral and hepatic safety remained uncertain. Treatment should be individualized based on patient and medication-related factors.

title: Neurotrophic regulation of lipid metabolism in Alzheimer's disease: Mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which lipid metabolic dysregulation is increasingly recognized as an important contributor to pathogenesis. Neurotrophic factors (NTFs), beyond their established roles in neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity, may also regulate lipid metabolism.ObjectiveTo summarize current evidence on lipid metabolic dysregulation in AD and evaluate the potential roles of major NTFs in regulating lipid homeostasis.MethodsExperimental, clinical, and translational studies addressing lipid metabolism, neurotrophic signaling, and their interactions in AD were reviewed, focusing on cholesterol, sphingolipid, and fatty acid metabolism and on BDNF, NGF, GDNF, CNTF, and Nrn1.ResultsDisturbances in cholesterol transport, sphingolipid and fatty acid metabolism, and high-density lipoprotein function may promote AD pathology by affecting membrane organization, synaptic plasticity, oxidative stress, insulin signaling, and amyloid-β and tau metabolism. BDNF, NGF, GDNF, CNTF, and Nrn1 may influence lipid-related processes through pathways including PI3K/Akt, AMPK, MAPK, and STAT3. However, evidence strength varies substantially among NTFs, and many proposed interactions are supported mainly by cellular, animal, or non-AD models.ConclusionsNeurotrophic signaling and lipid metabolism may form an interconnected regulatory network relevant to AD pathophysiology. This concept may support future biomarker and therapeutic research, but it should currently be regarded as a hypothesis-generating framework requiring direct validation in human AD and well-characterized AD models.

title: Improving the clinical trial landscape for Parkinson syndromes in Germany.
abstract: Germany has a longstanding tradition of excellence in neuroscience and Parkinson's research, supported by outstanding academic institutions, specialized clinical centers, and a strong scientific community. Building on this strong foundation, the country now has the opportunity to transform its clinical research landscape into a more integrated ecosystem for Parkinson syndromes. Despite major advances in molecular understanding, biomarker development, and therapeutic innovation, important structural, regulatory, financial, and organizational barriers continue to limit the full translational potential of German Parkinson research. Participants in an expert workshop identified identify recurring challenges, including fragmented trial infrastructures, slow and bureaucratic regulatory procedures, insufficient funding for investigator-initiated clinical research, limited integration of patient organizations, and suboptimal patient recruitment pathways. This workshop-derived perspective outlines a strategic framework to elevate Germany from a country with excellent individual centers to a globally competitive and integrated hub for innovative Parkinson clinical research. Key recommendations include transforming the German Parkinson Study Group into a nationally coordinated, service-oriented trial network; establishing centralized digital and regulatory infrastructures; diversifying public and philanthropic funding; implementing platform and observational trial structures; strengthening incentives for participating centers; and enhancing patient engagement through national registries, decentralized trial approaches, real-world data based evidence surveillance, and systematic integration of patient organizations. The authors argue that Germany must move beyond isolated university-based structures toward a nationally coordinated and highly efficient research ecosystem capable of rapidly delivering disease-modifying and precision medicine trials. Such a transformation could strengthen Germany's international position in neurodegenerative disease research and accelerate therapeutic innovation for patients with Parkinson syndromes.

title: Evaluation of harmonization methods to mitigate assay and cohort effects in plasma p-tau217.
abstract:
The growing number of assay platforms measuring blood-based biomarkers (BBMs) for Alzheimer's disease (AD) has introduced challenges in interpretability and comparability across assays. Differences across studies also limit comparability of data. To address these challenges, a systematic evaluation of harmonization methods is needed to support BBM data integration within or across studies.
Two multisite studies, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI, n = 219) and Human Connectome Project (HCP, n = 111), were used to evaluate harmonization methods for mitigating assay and cohort effects in plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) measurements. Methods included various normalization, regression, and standardization approaches, including the recently developed CentiMarker. Assay effects were evaluated using repeated-measures data across assay platforms within each cohort, whereas cohort effects were assessed using pooled ADNI and HCP data. Harmonization performance was evaluated using distributional statistics and downstream modeling of p-tau217.
Quantile normalization and quantile mapping methods were most effective for mitigating assay effects, whereas conditional quantile mapping performed best for pooled multi-cohort data. These methods also preserved biological variability. In contrast, simple means adjustment and reference-based Z-score standardization were least effective for mitigating assay effects, whereas simple means adjustment, Z-score standardization, and quantile normalization were least effective for mitigating cohort effects. CentiMarker had minimal impact on assay or cohort effects.
Based on our evaluation, we recommend (conditional) quantile mapping for p-tau217 studies integrating data across multiple assays or cohorts. In contrast, we caution against using CentiMarker and Z-score-based methods, as they limit comparability and do not effectively mitigate technical variability.

title: Restoration of StAR-governed neurosteroids with all-trans retinoic acid in alleviating cognitive deficits in a humanized amyloid-β knock-in mouse model of late-onset Alzheimer's disease: New insights into therapeutics.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial progressive neurodegenerative disorder of the elderly characterized by cognitive decline that involves diverse pathological processes. Aging, modulating neuronal instability, is the primary risk factor AD, resulting in dementia, for which a crucial neuropathological feature is the accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques wherein suppression of neurosteroids plays important roles. Neurosteroidogenesis gradually decreases during aging, and the regulation of neurosteroid biosynthesis is mediated by the steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR) protein. We demonstrate that treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (atRA, 20 mg/kg, 12-weeks) in humanized Aβ knock-in (hAbKI) mice (11-month old) resulted in increases in hippocampal StAR and sex neurosteroid (estradiol-17β/(E2) in females and testosterone in males) levels, when compared with controls. Elevated StAR and sex neurosteroid levels were associated with reductions in not only Aβ accumulation but also toxic soluble Aβ1-40 and Aβ1-42 peptides in both sexes, emphasizing an inverse correlation between neurosteroidogenesis and AD pathogenesis. Notably, atRA was capable of ameliorating cognitive impairments in both female and male hAbKI mice, as evaluated by Morris Water Maze analyses. These findings provide insights into the mechanistic events by which atRA restores neurosteroid instability, reduces neurotoxicity, and alleviates cognitive impairments in sex-specific hAbKI mice, demonstrating that retinoid therapy could serve as a novel target for the management of AD-related dementia for healthy aging.

title: Gut Microbiota in Alzheimer's Disease and Healthy Aging: Mechanisms, Prevention Strategies and Healthcare Burden.
abstract:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline associated with oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, tau neurofibrillary tangles, amyloid-beta plaque deposition, and metabolic dysfunction. Increasing evidence suggests that the gut microbiota plays an important role in AD pathogenesis through the microbiota-gut-brain axis. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the role of the gut microbiota in AD and healthy aging, with a particular focus on microbiota-targeted preventive and therapeutic strategies and their potential to influence disease progression.
Recent studies have demonstrated that alterations in gut microbial composition are closely associated with AD. Patients with AD commonly exhibit a reduced abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria and an increased prevalence of lipopolysaccharide-producing taxa, supporting a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis, systemic inflammation, and neurodegeneration. Emerging evidence indicates that dietary patterns, prebiotics, probiotics, synbiotics, postbiotics, and microbiota-based therapies, including fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), may beneficially modulate gut microbial composition and influence AD-related pathophysiological processes. In addition, lifestyle factors such as sleep quality and physical activity have been increasingly recognized for their interactions with the gut-brain axis and their potential to affect cognitive health. Current evidence highlights the gut microbiota as a promising therapeutic target in AD prevention and management. Microbiota-directed interventions, together with healthy dietary and lifestyle modifications, may help attenuate neuroinflammation, improve metabolic homeostasis, and delay cognitive decline. Furthermore, given the substantial global economic burden of AD, microbiota-focused preventive strategies may contribute not only to improving clinical outcomes but also to reducing long-term healthcare and societal costs. Future longitudinal and interventional studies are needed to establish causal relationships and determine the efficacy of microbiota-based therapies in AD.

title: Qualitative analysis of staff views on caring for inpatients with delirium and Parkinson's disease: Challenges, tensions and team working.
abstract: ObjectivesPeople with Parkinson's disease (PD) are at increased risk of delirium. Documentation of delirium is poor, with challenges in making a diagnosis due to overlapping symptoms. This study interviewed healthcare workers about their experiences of caring for inpatients with PD and delirium to explore their perspectives.DesignA qualitative study with semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis.ParticipantsTwelve healthcare staff, comprising five doctors and seven nurses.ResultsFour themes emerged: environmental pressures, relationship tensions, challenges and team working. We divided findings into those relevant to all inpatients with delirium and those specific to patients with PD and delirium. Environment pressures negatively impacted on all patients with delirium, and empathy was expressed for all carers/relatives. Staff anxiety was higher caring for patients with PD and relationship tensions occurred with juxtaposition of staff delirium expertise and patient/carer lived experience of PD. PD specific challenges were PD medications and a reciprocal relationship between diagnostic overshadowing and identifying the cause of delirium. Roles of ward nursing team to identify acute changes and doctors to identify and diagnose delirium in all patients was clearly defined.ConclusionsThis study identified knowledge gaps and lack of confidence specific to patients with delirium and PD. We recommend clearer definition of delirium superimposed on PD, with education and training on its complexity, alongside inclusion of expert-by-experience teaching. Future study of patient and carer views will help better understand the relationship tensions and how we can improve patient care and experiences.

title: Antithetical roles of tau in hippocampal long-term synaptic depression in rats versus mice.
abstract: Synaptic dysfunction is a primary feature of tauopathies, a group of major neurodegenerative diseases that includes Alzheimer's disease. However, the normal synaptic functions of tau are poorly understood. Since rats provide advantages over mice for understanding human tau, such as expressing six tau isoforms and showing more robust signs of tau pathology, as well as offering a richer behavioural repertoire, we developed a tau knockout (Mapt KO) rat line. We primarily investigated the impact of tau elimination on long-term synaptic depression (LTD)-a form of synaptic weakening that tau mediates in mice. Low-frequency stimulation of hippocampal Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses revealed a robust enhancement of LTD in Mapt KO rats relative to WT littermates. In contrast, in interleaved experiments, Mapt KO mice exhibited reduced LTD compared to WT littermates, in line with previous reports. Together, our findings demonstrate a species-dependent role for endogenous tau in regulating hippocampal LTD, promoting it in mice yet constraining it in rats. Therefore, the functions of tau are not necessarily conserved in rodents, underscoring the importance of animal model choice.

title: Metabolic Dyshomeostasis, neuroinflammation, and glymphatic clearance deficits as convergent drivers of Alzheimer's disease: an exposome-based conceptual framework for prevention.
abstract: The repeated failures of anti-amyloid therapies in Alzheimer's disease (AD) have exposed critical limitations of the linear amyloid cascade hypothesis and underscored the need for a broader etiological framework. The objective of this review is to synthesise mechanistic evidence for an exposome‑based model of sporadic AD that integrates metabolic, inflammatory, and sleep/circadian contributions to brain aging. Epidemiological evidence indicates that up to 40% of AD risk is attributable to modifiable environmental and lifestyle factors. These factors, collectively termed the aging exposome, represent the cumulative measure of external exposures and the body's biological responses across the lifespan. The central hypothesis is that sporadic AD emerges from the synergistic convergence of three interconnected exposome domains, metabolic dyshomeostasis, chronic neuroinflammation, and sleep/circadian disruption, which collectively lower the threshold for clinical dementia through shared molecular hubs like NF‑κB, mTOR, and ER stress. Central to this model is brain insulin resistance, which impairs cerebral glucose utilization, compromises mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, and disrupts lipid homeostasis via ceramide/sphingomyelin imbalance, collectively driving bioenergetic failure, oxidative stress, and enhanced amyloid-β production. Concurrently, peripherally derived and central inflammatory signals prime microglia, upregulate β-secretase (BACE1), and activate complement-mediated synaptic pruning, while emerging evidence suggests that sleep fragmentation and circadian misalignment are hypothesized to reduce glymphatic clearance and sustain BACE1 elevation, although direct causal evidence in humans remains limited. These ostensibly disparate pathways are integrated by shared molecular hubs, NF-κB, mTOR, and endoplasmic reticulum stress, which establish a self-reinforcing vicious cycle that selectively damages the hippocampus and default mode network. This cumulative aging exposome burden exerts its greatest impact during the midlife metabolic storm window (ages 40-60) and exhibits sex-specific vulnerability. Collectively, metabolic, inflammatory, and sleep deficits amplify each other via shared hubs; midlife is a critical, sex‑specific vulnerability window; and multi‑domain prevention is rational, though causal proof requires exposome‑wide and pragmatic trials. This reframes sporadic AD as an exposome‑driven syndrome, favoring simultaneous metabolic, immune, and sleep interventions over single‑target approaches.

title: The GBA1-related variant rs12411216 is Associated with Motor and Non-Motor Impairments and Unfavorable Progression in Parkinson's Disease: A Five-Year Longitudinal Study.
abstract: We investigated four regulatory single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) related to genes previously implicated in the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (rs76904798 and rs6581622 (LRRK2), rs356182 (SNCA), and rs12411216 (GBA1)) in order to assess their association with the clinical heterogeneity of Parkinson's disease. In a five-year observational study, 518 patients stratified by genotype were analyzed for cognitive, neuropsychiatric, motor, and other clinical signs.The rs356182 (SNCA) variant showed a modest association with disease traits, including significant associations with anxiety (HAMILTON scale). Conversely, the regulatory GBA1-related variant rs12411216 demonstrated a robust pleiotropic association with earlier disease onset, more severe motor impairment, and a broad spectrum of non-motor impairments, including anxiety, depression, impulsive-compulsive behaviors, and cognitive deficits. Longitudinal analyses revealed that patients homozygous for the rs12411216 AA genotype exhibited the most unfavorable progression across multiple domains, suggesting a faster neurocognitive decline.These findings suggest that the distinct pleiotropic effects of the GBA1-related variant rs12411216 contribute significantly to the clinical heterogeneity of PD by shaping unfavorable motor and neuropsychiatric progression trajectories. While the longitudinal design provides new evidence for genotype-dependent patterns, further functional studies are needed to confirm the proposed mechanistic link.

title: Multilingual Dementia Training for Paid Caregivers: A RE-AIM Mixed-Methods Evaluation.
abstract:
This study evaluated the IHSS+ ADRD Training Project, a multilingual intervention for caregivers serving individuals living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) through California's In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) program, using the RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) framework.
A quasi-experimental, mixed-methods evaluation was conducted from July 2019 to June 2024 across Alameda and Los Angeles counties. By applying the RE-AIM framework, Reach and Effectiveness dimensions were assessed through surveys completed by 488 caregivers in English (n = 297), Spanish (n = 102), and Chinese (n = 89) at pre-training, post-training, and 3-month follow-up. Caregivers were diverse among English speakers (38% Black/African American, 23% Hispanic/Latino, and 20% Asian), averaged 49.9 years old, and were predominantly women (88%). Quantitative measures assessed dementia knowledge, self-efficacy, distress, and depression. Qualitative interviews with stakeholders (n = 11) and open-ended caregiver survey responses explored Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance dimensions.
RE-AIM findings demonstrated: Reach across diverse caregiver populations in multilingual formats; Effectiveness with significant improvements in dementia knowledge and self-efficacy sustained at 3-month follow-up, plus 88-99% satisfaction; Adoption facilitated by union partnership; Implementation successfully transitioned to virtual delivery during COVID-19 despite technology barriers; and Maintenance supported by increased caregiver confidence, self-care awareness, and stress management skills, though sustainability required ongoing funding.
Language-concordant training produced meaningful, sustained improvements across a diverse paid caregiver workforce, demonstrating its value as an equity strategy in home care workforce development. While virtual delivery was feasible and cost-effective, long-term success depends on securing dedicated funding and reliable technology infrastructure.

title: Caregiver-provider relationship quality and health outcomes in family caregivers of people living with dementia.
abstract:
Family caregivers of individuals with Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) work with healthcare providers to ensure effective care coordination on behalf of the care recipient. However, challenges within the caregiver-healthcare provider relationship are common and may contribute to poor caregiver health outcomes. This study examined the impact of perceived quality of the relationship between family caregivers and healthcare providers and the caregivers' daily mental health symptom burden (depressive symptoms, anxiety, and stress).
The study included 228 family caregivers who lived with and provided unpaid care to a family member with dementia. Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMM) were developed to assess whether the caregiver-provider relationship was associated with caregiver daily depressive symptoms, daily anxiety, and daily stress.
Of 228 caregivers, 82% were female, 84% were spouses or partners of the care recipient, and 9% of caregivers were classified as living in poverty. Caregivers who rated their providers' affect (perceptions of being valued, respected, and emotionally supported) more positively reported lower daily depressive symptoms (β= -0.06, p = .001) and anxiety symptoms (β= -0.07, p < .001). The caregiver-provider relationship was not associated with daily stress experiences.
Findings from the study suggest that healthcare provider affect (perceptions of being valued, respected, and emotionally supported) may be a protective factor, especially against depressive symptoms and anxiety, and offer an avenue for future interventions. Integrating caregiver-provider relationship-informed practices into routine dementia care may help foster emotionally responsive, person- and family-centered care.

title: Closed-loop inhibitory metabotropic glutamate receptor gene therapy for focal refractory epilepsy.
abstract: Epilepsy is common and frequently refractory to anti-seizure medications. Although ablative surgery is effective when a seizure focus is identifiable, it is only suitable for a minority of patients because of risks of permanent neurological deficit. Several gene therapies for pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy are in development, including tools to achieve neuronal inhibition in response to pathological hyperactivity. Here we show that AAV9-mediated overexpression of the endogenous autoinhibitory metabotropic glutamate receptor mGlu2 (mGluR2, encoded by GRM2) prevents neuronal circuit hyperactivity ex vivo. Overexpression of mGlu2 in the ventral hippocampus suppressed chemoconvulsant-evoked seizures without affecting locomotion or behavioral markers of anxiety in naïve C57BL/6J mice. In a chronic model of pharmacoresistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, mGlu2 gene therapy profoundly attenuated spontaneous generalized seizures with no loss of efficacy over 8 weeks, and with concomitant improvements in comorbidities and survival. mGlu2 gene therapy avoids shortcomings of other strategies to suppress pathological hyperactivity in closed loop, relies on a mammalian effector transgene, and may thus be suitable for clinical translation.

title: Age-related differences in quality of life among people with epilepsy: an exploratory cross-sectional analysis of an Australian community sample.
abstract:
Epilepsy and ageing is an under-researched area particularly the Quality of Life (QoL) of older people with epilepsy (PWE). The effects of age on QoL needs an appreciation of the social and material context (Australia).
The Australian Epilepsy Longitudinal Study (AELS) into the Social Impact of Epilepsy is repeated every three years. Wave 6 of the AELS analysed the extent to which age differences explain QoL and particularly QoL outcomes for older PWE. For this the QOLIE-31 was used.
Older age led significantly to increasing QoL compared to younger adults. The dimension of QOLIE-31 Energy/fatigue and 3 other dimensions had the greatest difference between older and younger PWE. These were Social Function, Cognition and Emotional Well-being. Seizures led to lower QoL for older PWE and those 39-59 years compared to the youngest adults (aged 18-38 years) where seizures did not have a significant effect on QoL. Tangible supports of older people were significantly lower in their effect on QoL than for younger adults. For older PWE only, increased anti-seizure medication (ASM) use led significantly to lower QoL Living in the City benefitted 39-59 year olds in terms of affectionate support. This was not the case for younger or older PWE.
For older PWE certain issues need to be addressed such as comorbidities, depression and recognizing the value of social support. These should be in the context of the social impact of epilepsy.
