title: Clusters of modifiable dementia risk factors at mid-life and late-life and their association with incident dementia: A prospective cohort study of 246,968 adults.
abstract: BackgroundModifiable dementia risk factors rarely occur in isolation, yet their co-occurrence and clustering remain poorly characterized, limiting identification of high-risk individuals and development of targeted strategies.ObjectiveTo identify clusters of ten modifiable risk factors in mid-life (45-65 years) and late-life (>65 years), and to examine their association with incident dementia.MethodsData were drawn from the 2012 Dutch Public Health Monitor Survey (mid-life: n = 121,120; late-life: n = 125,848), with dementia follow-up through 2023. Ten modifiable risk factors: obesity, hypertension, diabetes, hearing loss, visual loss, physical inactivity, excessive alcohol consumption, smoking, loneliness, and depression, were used to derive clusters using latent class analysis. Cox proportional hazards models examined the association between late-life clusters and incident dementia.ResultsIn mid-life (mean age, 55.7 ± 6.2 years), four risk factor clusters were identified: cardiometabolic, substance use, psychosocial, and lower risk. In late-life (mean age, 73.9 ± 6.4 years), four clusters were identified: cardiometabolic, substance use, psychosocial and physically inactive, and lower risk. After adjustment for sociodemographic factors, the psychosocial and physically inactive cluster was associated with the highest hazard of dementia (hazard ratio (HR), 1.23; 95% CI, 1.16-1.32), followed by the substance use (HR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.09-1.24) and the cardiometabolic cluster (HR, 1.12; 95% CI, 1.07-1.18).ConclusionsDistinct risk factor clusters were identified at both mid-life and late-life; the psychosocial and physically inactive cluster carried the highest risk of dementia. These findings underscore the importance of considering risk factor clustering when designing targeted interventions to reduce dementia risk across the life course.

title: Neuropsychiatric symptoms in vascular cognitive impairment: A comparative study between CADASIL and sporadic small vessel disease.
abstract:
Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) are common in cerebral small vessel disease (SVD), but their patterns across genetic and sporadic forms remain incompletely characterized. We compared NPS prevalence, correlates, and caregiver distress in vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) due to cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL) and sporadic SVD.
Patients with VCI due to CADASIL or sporadic SVD were recruited from the Taiwan-Associated Genetic and Non-genetic Small Vessel Disease cohort. NPS were assessed using the Neuropsychiatric Inventory. Clinically significant NPS were defined as a frequency multiplied by severity score of 2 or higher. Group differences were examined using logistic regression adjusted for age and sex. Clinical and imaging correlates were analyzed separately for each group, and caregiver distress was evaluated using linear regression.
Among 245 VCI patients (100 CADASIL, 145 sporadic SVD), clinically significant NPS were frequent (72% vs. 63%, p = 0.133). Affective subsyndromes were more common in CADASIL (42% vs. 26%, p = 0.040). In CADASIL, dyslipidemia was associated with higher odds of NPS (adjusted OR = 4.63, p = 0.005), whereas anterior temporal involvement was associated with lower odds (adjusted OR = 0.29, p = 0.020). In sporadic SVD, dementia severity was the strongest correlate of NPS. Psychotic and apathy subsyndromes increased with dementia severity in both groups, whereas affective subsyndromes did not. Caregiver distress correlated strongly with symptom severity (Spearman's ρ = 0.42-0.70).
NPS are highly prevalent in VCI due to CADASIL and sporadic SVD, with affective symptoms particularly prominent in CADASIL.

title: Feasibility of a multidimensional interdisciplinary rehabilitation program for people with dementia and their informal primary caregivers - a randomized pilot trial with a caregiver focus.
abstract:
To improve the situation of informal caregivers, both supportive efforts for caregiver and rehabilitation for the person with dementia, may be needed. This randomized controlled pilot trial evaluated, among caregivers, the feasibility of a person-centred multidimensional interdisciplinary rehabilitation program for community-dwelling people with dementia that incorporated an education and support intervention for informal caregivers.
Informal caregivers were randomized alongside the person with dementia to an intervention group (n=36) or usual care (n=31). Multiprofessional team rehabilitation for individuals with dementia and support for caregivers, were offered for one 20-week and two 4-week follow-up periods after 5 and 14 months. Caregivers were offered assessments, participation in group sessions, and individual support. After the last group session, scheduled during the last four weeks of the 20-week period, a survey was distributed. Attendance at group sessions and uptake of individual support were recorded. Blinded assessments of caregiver burden (Caregiver Burden Scale, CBS), depressive symptoms (Geriatric Depression Scale 15-item version, GDS) and health-related quality of life (Short Form 36-Health Survey, SF-36), were performed at baseline and after 5, 12, 24, and 36 months.
Thirty-seven participants (56%) were spouses and 26 (39%) were adult children. Participation rate in assessments of outcomes at 36 months was 100% and 87% for intervention and control group in GDS and SF-36, respectively, and 69% and 61% for CBS, respectively. Missing data were primarily due to mortality. All caregivers in the intervention group (n=36) were assessed, and all received individual interventions by team staff. Twenty-three caregivers attended group sessions, and 21 completed a survey after the last session. Twenty (95%) caregivers reported increased knowledge about supporting the person with dementia, and 19 (90%) improved coping strategies. No significant differences were observed between groups in depressive symptoms or caregiver burden, yet differences in favour of the control group were seen in subscales of health-related quality of life at 24 and 36 months.
The program, combining rehabilitation for the person with dementia with caregiver support, seems feasible regarding caregivers' participation in the intervention and study evaluation, and thus further evaluation in an adequately powered randomized controlled trial seems relevant. A future definitive trial should evaluate continuous support over a longer period adapted to the caregiver and refine assessment procedures, including conducting assessments during ongoing interventions to provide greater insights into rehabilitation and caregiver-support effects.
The study protocol is published online 04/11/2015 at http://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN59155421.

title: Common mental health problems experienced by adolescents living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa: A scoping review.
abstract: Adolescents living with HIV (ALWH) carry a substantial burden of mental health problems, yet summary data remain limited. Previous reviews, particularly systematic reviews, have focused mainly on diagnosed disorders among adults or broader populations of young people living with HIV, while substance use and emotional and behavioural symptoms remain understudied and often underreported. This scoping review synthesized existing evidence on common mental health problems among ALWH aged 10-19 years in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). We searched five electronic databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Embase, and Open Access for Africa) and Google Scholar, and screened the bibliographic references of selected articles for additional studies. Search terms were combined using Boolean operators and organized into four concept categories: HIV, age, mental health, and region. Eligible studies were original, peer-reviewed research published in English between 2020 and 2026, conducted in SSA, and reporting on mental health among ALWH aged 10-19 years. The search yielded 427 records, of which 29 duplicates were removed. Of the 398 articles screened, 317 were excluded at the abstract stage and a further 57 after full-text review, leaving 24 articles for inclusion. The review identified six common mental health problems among ALWH in SSA: depressive disorders and symptoms, generalized anxiety, suicidality, emotional and behavioural problems, posttraumatic stress, and substance use problems. Depression and suicidality were the most frequently reported, whereas substance use, generalized anxiety, posttraumatic stress, and emotional and behavioural problems were less frequently reported. ALWH in SSA experience a range of mental health problems that may affect their well-being and engagement in HIV care. Routine mental health screening, prevention, and psychosocial support should be integrated into HIV care for this population. Strengthening integrated mental health and HIV services may help address unmet needs and improve health outcomes among ALWH in SSA.

title: Inherited and early-life vulnerability in functional neurological disorder and functional somatic symptoms: A retrospective cohort and case-control study from a large electronic health record database.
abstract:
Biological factors affecting motor, sensory, and integrative processing may predispose to functional neurological disorder (FND) and functional somatic symptoms. While early-life influences have traditionally been conceptualized within psychological frameworks, the contribution of early-life biological vulnerabilities to symptom expression remains unclear.
Using TriNetX, a large electronic health records database, we assessed proportions of inherited, congenital, perinatal, and neurodevelopmental diagnoses, capturing a range of early-life conditions. We compared 188,868 individuals with FND and 406,202 with functional somatic symptoms to demographically matched migraine and depression cohorts. Subgroup analyses contrasted motor FND with functional seizures and system-predominant functional somatic symptom clusters (e.g. bowel and bladder) with the general cluster.
Compared with migraine and depression, individuals with FND and functional somatic symptoms showed higher proportions of multiple inherited and early-life vulnerability factors. Congenital and inherited conditions, including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (OR = 2.1-3.6 across comparisons), congenital musculoskeletal malformations (1.7-2.0), and chromosomal abnormalities (2.5-3.2), were more prevalent. Perinatal factors such as low birth weight (1.8-2.4) were enriched, alongside neurodevelopmental disorders, including intellectual disability (1.9-5.4) and autism spectrum disorder (1.2-3.5). Subgroup analyses revealed phenotype-specific patterns: joint hypermobility and musculoskeletal malformations were more common in functional motor disorder and musculoskeletal functional somatic symptoms, whereas neurodevelopmental disorders were enriched in functional seizures and the general functional somatic symptom cluster.
Inherited and early-life biological vulnerabilities were more common in FND and functional somatic symptom cohorts. Their prevalence differed among phenotypes. Our findings suggest that developmental variation in brain-body systems may influence the risk and clinical expression of functional symptoms.

title: Mental Health and Psychosocial Processes in Transgender and Gender Diverse Adults with Chronic Physical Illnesses: A Scoping Review.
abstract: Transgender and gender diverse (TGD) adults experience high rates of chronic physical illnesses (CPIs) and mental health difficulties, yet little is known about the psychosocial processes underlying this relationship. This scoping review aimed to map and synthesize the literature examining psychosocial factors associated with mental health among TGD adults living with CPIs. Following PRISMA-ScR and Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines, systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Google Scholar. Eligible qualitative and quantitative studies that investigated psychosocial processes and mental health outcomes among TGD adults with CPIs were included. Twenty-five studies met the eligibility criteria. Most were cross-sectional and focused on transgender women living with HIV. Minority stress-related experiences, including stigma, discrimination, trauma, and violence, were consistently associated with depression, anxiety, psychological distress, poorer quality of life, and reduced healthcare engagement. In contrast, social support, community connectedness, resilience, coping, mindfulness, and spirituality emerged as important protective factors. Few studies examined CPIs beyond HIV or biophysiological processes. Overall, the evidence highlights the central role of minority stress in shaping mental health among TGD adults with CPIs while revealing substantial gaps regarding diverse TGD populations, non-HIV chronic illnesses, and transdiagnostic and biopsychosocial mechanisms that should be prioritized in future research.

title: Positive-affective and negative-cognitive brain-behavior axes in clinical high risk for psychosis.
abstract:
Individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR) present with heterogeneous combinations of positive, negative, and affective symptoms, cognitive difficulties, and functional impairment. However, reproducible multivariate links between this multidomain phenotype and brain morphology remain limited. This study explored the multivariate brain-behavior associations in CHR using a data-driven approach.
Baseline data from 720 CHR participants from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership® Schizophrenia program (AMP® SCZ) were analyzed using sparse canonical correlation analysis to identify associations between 95 regional brain volumes and 28 behavioral variables indexing symptoms, cognition, and functioning. Generalizability was tested using leave-one-network-out cross-validation (PRoNET and PRESCIENT), and stability was assessed using bootstrapping and leave-one-site-out analyses. Associations with demographic, clinical and site-related variables were examined.
Two brain-behavior dimensions generalized across networks. A positive-affective axis (r=0.21-0.23), linking higher depression, anxiety/stress, positive symptoms and anhedonia with predominantly frontal-cingulate-insular volume reductions and relatively larger corpus callosum and putamen volumes. This axis was associated with comorbid depression, cannabis use and family history of depression or affective psychosis. A negative-cognitive axis (r=0.17-0.18) linked greater asociality, alogia, emotional withdrawal, blunted affect, and motor retardation, poorer cognition and functioning with reduced cerebellar and parietal volumes, and relatively larger lateral ventricles and corpus callosum. This axis was associated with lower IQ and poorer premorbid adjustment.
Two partially dissociable brain-behavior dimensions were identified: a positive-affective axis capturing the co-expression of affective and attenuated positive symptoms, and a negative-cognitive axis suggestive of neurodevelopmental vulnerability.

title: The exposome in schizophrenia: A systematic review of environmental risk indices.
abstract:
Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder resulting from the dynamic interaction between genetic vulnerability and multiple environmental exposures acting across the lifespan. The exposome framework has emerged as a comprehensive approach to capture cumulative and interdependent environmental risk, moving beyond traditional single-factor models.
A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines to synthesize current evidence on the development, validation, and application of exposome-based indices in schizophrenia and psychotic spectrum disorders. The search was performed in PubMed, ScienceDirect and SciELO for studies published between 2005 and 2026. Eligible studies included original research and reviews integrating multiple environmental exposures into cumulative or latent risk models. Methodological quality and risk of bias were independently assessed using the ROBINS-E tool. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261286786).
Thirty-three studies were included, identifying five primary composite indices such as the Exposome Score for Schizophrenia (ES-SCZ), Maudsley Environmental Risk Score (ERS), Early Adversity Scale for Schizophrenia (EAS-Sz), Polyenviromic Risk Score (PERS), and Korea-Polyenvironmental Risk Score (K-PERS-I). Across studies, higher cumulative environmental burden was consistently associated with increased psychosis risk, greater symptom severity, cognitive impairment, and poorer functional outcomes. Models using empirical weighting or context-specific calibration generally showed better performance than simple additive approaches.
Cumulative environmental burden can be operationalized through structured exposome-based indices, several of which demonstrate moderate discriminatory capacity for schizophrenia and psychosis-related outcomes. However, substantial methodological heterogeneity and limited external validation currently restrict clinical applicability, underscoring the need for harmonization and rigorous cross-cohort validation to advance translational utility.

title: Twenty-five years of progress in Parkinson's disease research: from dopamine replacement to biological definition and regenerative therapy.
abstract: The first quarter of the twenty-first century has transformed Parkinson's disease (PD) from a predominantly motor, dopamine-deficiency syndrome into a heterogeneous multisystem disorder defined across clinical, genetic and molecular dimensions. This overview follows the trajectory of these advances from the historical foundations established prior 2000 to present concepts of prodromal disease, progression, biological classification and precision medicine. Epidemiological work has established PD as the fastest-growing major neurological disorder, while systematic characterization of non-motor symptoms has shifted diagnosis and attention beyond the nigrostriatal system in PD research. Imaging has progressed from exclusionary structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to quantitative susceptibility, diffusion and molecular approaches, although no single imaging biomarker yet provides a stand-alone diagnosis of PD. The discovery of α-synuclein gene mutations and its presence as protein in Lewy bodies and neurites connected genetics, protein aggregation and selective neuronal vulnerability. Seed amplification assays (SAA) now enable robust detection of pathological α-synuclein in cerebrospinal fluid and have catalysed biologically anchored staging proposals. At the same time, negative phase 2 antibody against α-synuclein trials illustrate the challenges of target engagement, disease heterogeneity and intervention timing. Genetics and cell biology have placed lysosomal proteostasis, in particular glucocerebrosidase 1 (GBA1) dependent pathways, at the center of disease-modification strategies. Dopaminergic therapy remains extraordinarily effective symptomatically, with continuous delivery systems extending its utility for intermediate and late stages of the disease, whereas cell replacement has re-entered clinical development through standardized pluripotent-stem-cell-derived midbrain dopaminergic progenitors. The next phase of PD research will depend less on a single unifying mechanism than on integrating molecular state, the pattern of neuronal injury, clinical phenotype and individual trajectory to select the right intervention at the right biological stage.

title: Spatially Resolved Multiplex Detection of Cytokines in Parkinson's Disease Rat Brain via CRISPR/Cas Biosensing.
abstract: The ability to accurately quantify localized neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative biomarkers in vivo is critical for enabling the early diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD). Here, we demonstrate a strategy for localized neuroinflammation quantification using an implantable glass-fiber-based CRISPR/Cas immunosensor. When interfaced with a portable fluorescence detector, our platform enables the spatially resolved multiplex detection of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and alpha-synuclein (α-syn) in the PD rat brain. The sensor surface was modified with functionalized liquid metal nanoparticles to enable antibody immobilization and long-term in vivo operation. This method demonstrated high specificity, excellent linearity in artificial cerebrospinal fluid (R2 > 0.91), sustained surface stability over 28 days, good biocompatibility with PC12 cells, and selective antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus. Following cannula implantation into the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) of a 6-hydroxydopamine-induced PD rat model, the functionalized glass fiber enabled repeated, minimally invasive biomarker sampling at 6, 12, and 24 h postimplantation. Systemic inflammation induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) triggered marked elevations in TNF-α, IL-6, and α-syn, peaking at 6 h post-LPS. This implantable fiber-based biosensing method offers a promising reliable approach for early PD diagnosis, disease progression tracking, and investigation of neuroimmune interactions in neurodegenerative diseases in a point-of-care scenario.

title: Epidemiological comparison of cirrhosis to other long-term health conditions in the United Kingdom.
abstract:
Although cirrhosis is a serious long-term health condition (LTC), it tends to receive little attention from healthcare policymakers. Here, we sought to describe how cirrhosis compares to other LTCs to inform priority-setting discussions.
We analysed data from the Our Future Health (OFH) study, a cohort of ∼1.7 million individuals from England, United Kingdom. Self-reported diagnosis status for cirrhosis and 15 benchmark LTCs (including type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, Parkinson's disease, chronic kidney disease, schizophrenia, and stage 4 cancer) were ascertained from the enrolment questionnaire. Each LTC was profiled with respect to: sociodemographic characteristics; mortality; comorbidity burden; and late diagnosis. Furthermore, information on each LTC's trajectory (i.e., increasing, stable, or decreasing over time) was determined from background mortality data over the last decade.
The study cohort included 1,613,777 participants, of whom 2,606 (0.2%) reported a diagnosis of cirrhosis. Mortality elevation for participants with cirrhosis versus without was substantial (HR: 7.46; P<0.001, with adjustment for age/sex) and comparable to dementia (HR:7.60), stage 4 cancer (HR:7.06), whilst higher than schizophrenia (HR:4.46) and heart failure (HR:4.01). People with cirrhosis had more co-existing health conditions/diseases than other LTCs (i.e., elevated prevalence for 58/145 distinct health conditions; second only to stage 4 cancer). Area-based deprivation score was third highest for cirrhosis, behind COPD and schizophrenia. Late diagnosis of cirrhosis was commonplace, with <15% of new-onset liver failure reporting cirrhosis at enrolment. Cirrhosis also exhibited an upward trajectory, with mortality increasing by ∼20% in the last decade.
Cirrhosis is an anomaly LTC with respect to its deprivation, comorbidity, mortality, upward trajectory, and late diagnosis profile. Our data provide comparative evidence to inform priority-setting discussions with policymakers.
Various levers are available to policy makers for reducing incidence of liver cirrhosis. However, other health conditions are often prioritised by policy makers ahead of cirrhosis; the decision-making process around this is not always transparent nor grounded in evidence. This study explores the characteristics of cirrhosis relative to other long-term conditions through a public-health lens. Our findings may guide priority-setting discussions between policy makers, advocates and other stakeholders and may shift current discourse onto a more empirical footing.

title: Pharmacist role in transforming Alzheimer's care: Anti-amyloid therapy experience at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.
abstract:
Anti-amyloid infusion therapies are a new and complex treatment option for patients with Alzheimer's disease. Use of lecanemab or donanemab requires specific diagnostic criteria and frequent ongoing monitoring that requires in-depth coordination of care. We describe how neurology clinical pharmacists were an integral part of adoption of anti-amyloid therapy at our institution. With implementation of this service by pharmacists, we describe the impact on patient outcomes for those receiving anti-amyloid infusions and several aspects of impact on the health system as a whole that pharmacists should anticipate with these complex infusions.
Neurology clinical pharmacists dedicated to infusions therapies are responsible for many aspects of use of anti-amyloid therapies, including order entry, patient counseling, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) registry submission, infusion scheduling, and coordination of magnetic resonance imaging. At our institution, the first year of anti-amyloid infusions included 58 patients starting infusions. Safety and adverse effects, including amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, were similar to those previously reported in the primary literature. The majority of patients utilized Medicare as their primary coverage for infusions, and we describe successful navigation of the unique CMS registry requirement for billing.
Adoption of anti-amyloid therapies by a health system requires unique aspects of coordination not previously encountered. Clinical pharmacists are positioned to successfully coordinate care for patients receiving anti-amyloid infusions.

title: LncRNA OIP5-AS1 is Involved in Alzheimer's Disease by Targeting miR-7-5p to Regulate Microglial Inflammation, Polarization and Oxidative Stress.
abstract: Diagnostic methods for Alzheimer's disease (AD) are limited due to cost and invasiveness, while long non-coding RNA has been identified as a promising candidate as a biomarker for AD due to the fact of easy analysis. The study aimed to explore the significance of OIP5-AS1 in AD progression. OIP5-AS1 expression in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of 107 AD subjects and 81 healthy individuals was evaluated by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). The association between OIP5-AS1 and AD severity was evaluated by the correlation analysis and chi-square test. Risk factors for AD were analyzed by multivariate logistic regression analysis. title: A five-gene mitochondrial-lipid metabolism signature for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis identified by machine learning and validated in independent cohorts.
abstract: BackgroundMitochondrial dysfunction and lipid metabolism dysregulation represent early key events in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet integrated transcriptomic signatures combining these two biological processes for AD diagnosis remain poorly defined.ObjectiveThis study aimed to construct and validate a mitochondrial-lipid metabolism (MLM) gene-based diagnostic classifier for AD using machine-learning approaches and explore its underlying biological mechanisms.MethodsTwo public GEO datasets GSE5281 (training) and GSE28146 (independent validation) were included. Candidate MLM genes were retrieved from MSigDB. Differentially expressed MLM genes were screened by limma, followed by two-step feature selection with LASSO regression and random forest. Four machine-learning algorithms were compared. Model performance was evaluated by AUC, calibration, decision-curve analysis and subgroup analysis across AD severity. GSVA and hypergeometric test were applied for mechanistic exploration.ResultsA five-gene signature (SDR16C5, EGR1, ASAH2B, HIP1R, CKMT1B) was finally identified. Logistic regression model achieved 5-fold cross-validated AUC of 0.953 in training cohort and AUC = 0.892 (95%CI:0.768-1.000) in validation cohort. GSVA revealed close correlations between this signature with oxidative stress, synaptic dysfunction and apoptosis pathways.ConclusionsThis validated five-gene MLM signature exhibits favorable diagnostic performance for AD and reflects disturbed mitochondrial-lipid metabolic network. It provides a promising transcriptomic biomarker for AD diagnosis.

title: The role of polysomnography in Parkinson's disease: objective sleep assessment and clinical indications.
abstract: Sleep disorders (SDs) are highly prevalent in Parkinson's disease (PD), affecting up to 80% of patients during the disease and significantly contributing to impaired quality of life, cognitive decline, motor worsening, fall risk, and increased caregiver burden. Polysomnography (PSG) remains the gold standard for objective sleep assessment in PD and plays a central role in differential diagnosis and therapeutic planning. This review examines the spectrum of SDs identifiable by PSG, including rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD), obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), periodic limb movements in sleep, and alterations in sleep architecture. Video-polysomnography (v-PSG) is essential for confirming REM sleep without atonia (RWA), which is the electrophysiological hallmark of RBD and a recognized prodromal marker of synucleinopathies. Also, PSG quantifies the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), oxygen desaturation burden, and sleep fragmentation, parameters associated with cognitive impairment and disease progression. While home sleep apnea testing (HSAT, type 3) may be useful for selected cases with high suspicion of OSA, comprehensive in-laboratory (type 1) PSG provides superior diagnostic accuracy, particularly in patients with complex or overlapping sleep disturbances. Integrating objective sleep evaluation into routine PD management is crucial to identify treatable comorbidities, improve prognostic stratification, and optimize motor and non-motor outcomes.

title: Education reduces dementia incidence and mitigates genetic risk.
abstract: There is little causal evidence on factors that can protect individuals against Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) risk. We study the causal effect of education on ADRD, exploiting a regression discontinuity generated by a compulsory schooling reform. ADRD was ascertained based on medical history, hospital records, and death registries, addressing concerns about selective sample attrition. We find that education reduces incidence of ADRD. Using molecular genetic data, we show that the reform weakened the relationship between genetics and ADRD incidence, implying genetic risk of dementia is not immutable and can be modified by social policy.

title: Translational control of microglial metabolism, inflammatory responses, and survival by the eIF4E-binding proteins.
abstract: In Alzheimer's disease (AD), activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes microglial neuroprotective functions by engaging multiple cell receptors. However, the relevant downstream effectors are not fully understood. mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) promotes mRNA translation by phosphorylating and inactivating eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 and 2 (4E-BP1/2), which are expressed in microglia. 4E-BP1 levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are elevated in AD and correlate with markers of microglial reactivity and disease progression. Using linear regression analysis, we found that elevated CSF 4E-BP1 levels strengthen the association between soluble TREM2 levels and neurodegeneration in amyloid-positive individuals. To investigate the underlying mechanism, we performed in vitro experiments demonstrating that amyloid-β inactivated 4E-BP1 in murine microglia. The mTOR-mediated inactivation is highly dependent on Spleen Tyrosine Kinase (SYK) signaling and repeated exposure to amyloid-β impaired this process, whereas prolonged exposure increased 4E-BP1 levels in microglia. Deletion of 4E-BP1/2 resulted in increased mitochondrial mass and oxidative phosphorylation, reduced pro-inflammatory signaling, and protected microglia from amyloid-induced apoptosis. Thus, impaired 4E-BP1 inactivation-due to reduced mTOR signaling or excess 4E-BP1-disrupts immune resolution, leading to metabolic exhaustion and microglial cell death. We identify the SYK-mTORC1-4E-BP1 signaling axis as a key regulator of microglial mitochondrial biogenesis and immune resolution in AD.

title: Amelioration of early pathological changes in the 3xTg-AD mouse model: Mechanism of action of the Chinese herbal formula Tianqi Granules.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline. This study investigated the effects of the Chinese herbal formula Tianqi Granules on early pathological progression in the 3xTg-AD mouse models and investigated the underlying mechanisms. After 31 days of Tianqi Granule treatment initiated at 5 months of age, Tianqi Granules-treated mice showed improved performance in the open-field test, novel object recognition test, and Morris water maze test. Amyloid deposition and glial activation were attenuated, and immunoreactivity for interleukin-1β and LC3 was reduced. Hippocampal transcriptome sequencing at multiple time points showed that, in untreated mice, early pathological progression occurred in three successive phases, with the dominant processes shifting from compensatory programs to failing homeostasis and subsequently to degenerative changes. Tianqi Granule treatment was associated with a three-phase response centered on the restoration of homeostasis and involving proteostasis, nuclear processes, lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, and redox-related pathways. Multiple biological domains were engaged rather than a single target. In males, an interferon-related program associated with Irf7 was induced early and shifted in the opposite direction under Tianqi Granule treatment during the same time window. Network pharmacology identified OPRK1 as the only candidate target shared by both sexes, making it a potential target for future investigation. These findings suggest that Tianqi Granule modulates the pathology of Alzheimer's disease through coordinated actions on multiple targets and may influence systemic metabolic homeostasis, providing experimental support for early therapeutic intervention in Alzheimer's disease.

title: Machine Learning Approach Investigating Differentially Expressed Genes Associated With Parkinson's Disease on Exposure to Pesticides Through Nutritional Uptake.
abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disease, with environmental exposures such as pesticides implicated as contributing risk factors. While ensemble machine learning (ML) models have shown promise in identifying discriminating genes from transcriptomic data, their generalizability across heterogeneous toxicogenomic datasets remains poorly characterized. Here, we present a robust statistical pipeline as the primary framework for identifying PD-associated, pesticide-responsive differentially expressed genes (DEGs), developed in direct response to the limitations observed in an ensemble ML approach. The ensemble model, combining individual ML models, Random Forest, Logistic Regression and Gradient Boosting was first trained on merged GEO transcriptomic datasets following normalization and feature selection (SelectKBest, ANOVA F-test, StandardScaler). Initially, an ROC AUC (Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve) of 0.734 with a cross-validation (CV) AUC of 0.632 was obtained with an average AUC of 0.806 +/- 0.106 across 10 different splits of train/test data points. The confusion matrix and PCA plots indicated the presence of strong batching effects driving these results. Batch correction improved CV AUC to 0.864 ± 0.142, yet cross-dataset validation collapsed to an ROC AUC of 0.523 ± 0.040, with the model consistently predicting a single class-indicating the ensemble had learned technical artefacts rather than generalizable biological signal. Given this failure of ML generalizability, an alternate, statistically grounded pipeline was developed that relied on domain-specific analysis of transcriptomics data. Differential expression was assessed using limma to determine the extent and significance of gene expression changes across pesticide-exposure datasets. Hub genes were identified through protein-protein interaction network analysis, and their associated pathways were enriched and validated against existing literature. The protein-protein interaction network was constructed and hub genes {Citation}with their respective pathways were identified. The fact that pesticides contribute to the progression of PD has been established by multiple studies. This study highlights the necessity of statistically rigorous, domain-informed approaches over black-box ML methods for identifying reliable, biologically meaningful DEGs-representing a novel methodological comparison not previously explored in pesticide-associated PD biomarker research.

title: Practical consideration for the application of continuous glucose monitoring in older adults with insulin treated diabetes.
abstract: The increased prevalence of diabetes among older individuals presents challenges for delivery of effective care for each older person with diabetes, for their families, and for healthcare providers. Along with established risks for microvascular and macrovascular disease, diabetes in older adults is also associated with risk factors for cognitive impairment and dementia, depression and physical frailty. Many of these risk factors are linked to hypoglycaemia, which in turn can be related to polypharmacy and overprescribing in older individuals. Use of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) technology is proven to prevent hypoglycaemia and can mitigate many averse outcomes of frailty, both in type 1 diabetes (T1D and type 2 diabetes (T2D). Similarly, use of CGM improves glucose stability, reducing risks for vascular complications of diabetes. Intrinsic capacity (IC) is a concept used in geriatric medicine to provide an objective composite of physical and mental capacities that an older individual can draw on. Reduced IC is associated with a number of CGM metrics, including time in range (TIR), time above range (TAR), rather than hypoglycaemia. Use of CGM can also facilitate telemedicine for adults with diabetes and frailty, reducing the burden of clinic attendance and increasing the frequency of healthcare contacts, further increasing the quality of care and quality of life for older individuals with diabetes. Given the significant benefits, the application of CGM alongside geriatric principles can be proposed to improve overall care and outcomes for people with diabetes.

title: Circadian rhythms in health and disease.
abstract: Circadian rhythms, serving as a crucial temporal bridge linking neural activity and pathological biology, are regulated by central pacemaker neurons to maintain cellular homeostasis and coordinate diverse biological processes. Circadian rhythm disruption is closely associated with various diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Circadian rhythms are controlled by core clock genes, such as BMAL1 and CLOCK, modulating numerous physiological processes, encompassing metabolism, immune responses, neural activity, and hormone regulation. Circadian rhythms disruptions arising from shift work, jet lag, or inconsistent sleep schedules are implicated in both the onset and progression of numerous diseases, notably Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The article highlights how circadian dysregulation alters cellular processes to potentially accelerate disease progression. Circadian disruption results in impaired immune function, further promoting disease development and resistance to treatment. Potential therapeutic applications based on circadian biology, such as chronotherapy and personalized medicine, are also discussed. Recent technological advances, embodied in wearable devices and omics approaches, are increasingly providing deeper insights into circadian biology. Further unveiling the role of circadian in health and disease opens new avenues for tailoring treatment timing to patients' biological rhythms, thereby enhancing therapeutic outcomes across various diseases. By bridging fundamental circadian mechanisms with clinical pathology, this review provides a roadmap for future chronotherapeutic interventions in precision medicine.

title: Discovery of an HDAC2-Selective Inhibitor via Enzyme-Inhibitor-Binding Thermodynamics/Kinetics as a Prospective Neurological Disorder Drug.
abstract: In this study, we identified KTT-1 (12) as an HDAC2-selective inhibitor through in vitro evaluations based on both thermodynamics and kinetics of the enzyme-inhibitor binding. This approach stands in sharp contrast to conventional drug discovery research, which usually focuses only on thermodynamics. An X-ray crystallography study on HDAC2 complexed with 12 in combination with quantum chemical calculations on model compounds suggested that the 2-furanyl group of 12 contributes to the selective HDAC2 inhibition. In our cellular assays, 12 preferentially inhibited HDAC2 over its highly homologous HDAC1 and promoted neurite outgrowth of neuro-2a cells. Furthermore, treatment of mice with 12 improved the memory and depression-like behavior of stress-vulnerable mice. The results indicate that 12 is a promising lead compound for neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and depression and demonstrate that inhibitor evaluations that combine enzyme-inhibitor-binding thermodynamics and kinetics are useful tools for drug discovery research.

title: Exploring the role of depression in the association between APOE ε4 and cognitive function: Evidence from the Brain Health Registry.
abstract:
Apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and associated with increased risk of depression. We examined whether depression modifies the association between APOE ε4 and cognition.
Using the Brain Health Registry (BHR), APOE ε4 status was determined by saliva-based genotyping. Depression and depression severity were self-reported as history of depression (yes/no), the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS; range 0-14), and Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9 range: 0-27). Cognitive function was measured via the Paired Associates Learning (PAL) test, including First Attempt Memory Score (FAMS) and Total Errors Adjusted (TEA). Linear regression estimated associations between APOE ε4, depression, and PAL (FAMS and TEA, separately) adjusted for age, gender, and education. An APOE ε4*depression interaction was tested. Inverse probability weights (IPW) were applied to address missingness.
Among 422 eligible participants, 25% were APOE ε4 carriers. Carriers were slightly younger than non-carriers (65 vs. 67 years, p = 0.025) with no other significant sociodemographic differences. GDS and PHQ-9 scores were right-skewed, and carriers had slightly lower medians (GDS: 1 vs. 2, p = 0.055; PHQ-9: 1 vs. 2, p < 0.001) but higher self-reported depression (18% vs. 14%, p = 0.3). APOE ε4 was associated with lower FAMS and higher TEA, but results were not statistically significant. Depression measures also showed non-significant associations with FAMS and TEA. No interactions were detected.
APOE ε4 and depression were non-significantly associated with cognition, and depression did not modify the association between APOE ε4 and cognitive function.

title: "Carrying the burden silently": A mixed-methods analysis of common mental health disorders among women caregivers living with HIV in Enugu, Nigeria.
abstract: Women caregivers living with HIV (WCLHIV) face a dual burden of managing their own health while caring for their families, increasing their vulnerability to mental health disorders. This study aimed to ascertain the prevalence and factors associated with common mental health disorders among WCLHIV in Enugu, Nigeria. A cross-sectional study employing a mixed method approach was conducted among 1,011 WCLHIV accessing anti-retroviral therapy in four tertiary health facilities in Enugu State, Nigeria. Quantitative data were obtained face-to-face using pre-tested, validated tools to assess the prevalence of depression, anxiety, stigma, and other psychological characteristics. Multivariate logistic regression identified significant risk factors of mental health disorders at a 95% confidence interval and p < 0.05. Four focus group discussions involving 35 WCLHIV explored factors impacting their mental well-being. Qualitative data were analyzed thematically using an inductive approach. Participants had a mean age of 44.3 (SD ± 8.44) years. The prevalence of depression and anxiety was 25.7% and 19.2%, respectively, while 79.0% reported high perceived stigma. Having primary education (AOR = 1.53; 95% CI: 1.06 -2.22), and low social support (AOR = 2.32; 95% CI: 1.11-5.07) were risk factors while low income (AOR = 0.42; 95% CI: 0.21-0.85), and low perceived stress (AOR = 0.05; 95% CI: 0.02-0.15) were protective of depression. Low perceived stress was protective of anxiety (AOR = 0.07; 95% CI: 0.02-0.22). Qualitative findings converged with quantitative data, highlighting the impact of stigma, poor social support, pill burden, fear of status disclosure, and financial strain on the mental health of WCLHIV.The prevalence of common mental health disorders was high among WCLHIV with a substantial proportion experiencing depression and anxiety, reflecting the significant impact of stigma, low social support, and stress. Targeted multi-level psychosocial interventions and community empowerment programs are needed to strengthen social support and reduce stigma among WCLHIV.

title: Belief in the 'Undetectable equals Untransmissible' statement and associations with stigma, mental health, and sexual satisfaction in people with HIV in the UK.
abstract:
The 'Undetectable equals Untransmissible' (U=U) statement is based on robust evidence. Spreading this message aims to reduce HIV stigma, increase antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence, and improve quality of life for people with HIV (PWH). Among PWH in the UK, we assessed the proportion believing U=U and its associations with HIV-related self-stigma, mental health, and sexual satisfaction.
Positive Voices 2022 is the largest UK national survey of PWH (April 2022-March 2023). Participants self-completed a questionnaire on socio-demographic, HIV-related, health, and lifestyle factors.
We assessed associations of demographic, socioeconomic, and HIV-related factors with belief in U=U (strong agreement with the statement " A person on HIV treatment with undetectable viral load cannot pass on HIV through sex )﻿, and associations of belief in U=U with HIV self-stigma, depression symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and sexual satisfaction (the latter among participants who had sex in the past 3 months) using logistic regression, unadjusted and adjusted for demographic group, age, and time on ART.
Four thousand five hundred and fifty-three people on ART were included: 2671 (59%) gay or bisexual MSM (GBMSM), 1104 (24%) women, 646 (14%) heterosexual men; 1100 (24%) participants of Black ethnicity; median (IQR) age 52 years (44-60). 4192 (92%) had heard of U=U; fewer (2906, 64%) believed it. Lack of belief in U=U was more common among older participants, heterosexuals, those with less education, those with financial hardship, and those without knowledge of their last viral load level. Lack of belief in U=U was associated with HIV-related self-stigma [adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 1.88, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.63-2.18], depression symptoms (aOR 1.33, 95% CI 1.13-1.56) anxiety symptoms (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.23-1.77), and lower odds of sexual satisfaction (physical pleasure: aOR 0.62, 95% CI 0.51-0.75; emotional satisfaction: aOR 0.72, 95% CI 0.60-0.87). With the exception of depression symptoms, these associations remained after additional adjustment for financial hardship. Patterns of association were similar among GBMSM compared to all other demographic groups combined.
Despite high awareness of U=U among PWH in UK, belief remains inadequate, especially in disadvantaged groups. Promoting this message could help combat HIV-related stigma and improve mental health.

title: A Cross-sectional Study for Estimation of Prevalence of Cognitive Impairment in Epileptic Patients.
abstract:
Cognitive impairment is a frequent, but frequently overlooked, complication of epilepsy that has a negative impact on patients' quality of life and functioning. Recurrent seizures and neurological factors can have a deleterious effect on multiple cognitive domains such as memory, attention, and executive function. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scale was used to assess cognitive impairment in patients with epilepsy in this study.
The objectives of this study were to estimate the prevalence of cognitive impairment in patients with diagnosed epilepsy for more than 2 years using the MoCA scale, assess cognitive function using the MoCA score in epilepsy patients, and determine the prevalence of cognitive impairment.
A hospital-based prospective observational study was conducted among 97 patients with epilepsy for 18 months. A MoCA scale (0-30) was used to evaluate cognitive function. Means and standard deviations were given for numerical variables, and frequencies and percentages were reported for categorical variables. The Fisher's exact test or Chi-square test was used for the analysis of categorical variables as appropriate.
The prevalence of cognitive impairment was significantly higher in the group with hypertension (45, 95.7%) than in the group without hypertension (40, 80.0%) (χ2 = 5.54, P = 0.02). The association between cognitive impairment and diabetes mellitus was not statistically significant. The associations with hypothyroidism, cerebrovascular accident, and ischemic heart disease were not statistically significant, as per Fisher's exact test (P = 0.99, 0.07, and 0.99, respectively).
Based on these findings, it is concluded that there is a need to consider cognitive impairment as an important and often unrecognized comorbidity with the overall disease burden of patients with epilepsy. The authors emphasize that it is crucial to include routine cognitive assessments in daily clinical practice.

title: Flavokawain A: a multi-targeted kava chalcone with diverse therapeutic potential.
abstract: Piper methysticum G. Forst., commonly known as Kava, is a culturally significant shrub native to the Pacific islands, including Fiji, Vanuatu, and Tonga. Flavokawain A is one of the primary non-kavalactone constituents found within its rhizomes. This review aims to provide a comprehensive and critical evaluation of the current state of research on Flavokawain A. Specifically, it aims to elucidate the diverse molecular mechanisms and signaling networks that drive its pharmacological effects, while assessing its viability as a multi-targeted therapeutic candidate for diverse diseases. Flavokawain A exhibits profound therapeutic potential across a spectrum of pathological conditions, including malignancy, chronic inflammation, myocardial infarction, and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. Evidence from in silico, in vitro and in vivo models suggests that Flavokawain A's efficacy is rooted in its ability to modulate key signaling hubs, notably the TGF-β1, NF-κB, PI3K/AKT, and Nrf2 pathways, as well as regulatory proteins like PRMT5, CDK2, and SKP2. These multi-target interactions underpin Flavokawain A's potent antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory properties, positioning it as a promising candidate for multifactorial disease management. FKA represents a versatile, multi-targeted potential therapeutic scaffold with a robust pharmacological profile. Its demonstrated anti-fibrotic, anti-inflammatory, and anti-proliferative activities across diverse disease models underscore its clinical potential. However, bridging the gap from bench to bedside requires rigorous translational studies and clinical trials to validate its safety, bioavailability, and therapeutic efficacy in human populations.

title: Morning lighting intervention reduces fatigue and improves sleep in Parkinson disease.
abstract: Fatigue and sleep disturbances are common in Parkinson Disease (PD) and significantly reduce quality of life, yet effective pharmacological treatments are limited. Light therapy offers a promising non-pharmacologic approach, but most lighting interventions have focused on improving sleep. Using a novel and easily administered morning lighting intervention, we previously demonstrated improvement in sleep duration. We have now extended the prior study through the addition of 23 individuals to investigate the intervention's effect on fatigue and sleep. In this single-arm intervention study, participants received morning light for 4 consecutive weeks from table or floor luminaires designed to deliver circadian-effective ambient light at home. Objective sleep was measured with wrist-worn actigraphy and subjective sleep, fatigue and mood were assessed using standardized questionnaires. Analysis of pre and post intervention data for the current cohort was performed separately as well as in combination with the 20 participants from the previously reported pilot study. For the 23 current participants, fatigue on the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-F) scale improved by 3.9 ± 1.00 points (p = 0.0026). While sleep duration increased by mean 21.3 ± 14.4 min, it was not statistically significant (p = 0.082). When combined with the 20 participants from the prior pilot study, significant improvement in fatigue by 2.8 ± 0.85 points (p = 0.0033) was observed and sleep duration was also significantly increased by 24.7 ± 10.4 min (p = 0.012). These findings support morning light as a novel intervention for fatigue in PD.

title: Assessing cognitive compensatory strategy use in epilepsy: Pilot validation of the everyday compensation questionnaire.
abstract:
Cognitive impairment is cited as one of the most consequential comorbidities of epilepsy. Cognitive difficulties may be managed using compensatory strategies. However, little is understood about how these strategies are used by adults with epilepsy. The Everyday Compensation (EComp) Questionnaire offers a means of assessing the use of these strategies but has only been validated for neurologically healthy older adults. The present study examined the preliminary psychometric properties of the EComp Questionnaire in epilepsy.
37 adults with focal epilepsy participating in a randomized controlled trial of a cognitive prehabilitation program completed the EComp Questionnaire, Quality of Life Epilepsy Inventory-31 (QOLIE-31), and the Instrumental Activities of Daily-Living Scale (IADL-C) at baseline and follow-up. Analyses included evaluation of internal consistency, construct validity, test-retest reliability, and item-level performance.
Across 20 imputed datasets, the EComp Questionnaire demonstrated acceptable Cronbach's α values. Test-retest ICCs were moderate (0.50-.58) but imprecise, with 95 % CIs spanning poor to good reliability. Correlations between the EComp Questionnaire and the IADL-C (ρ = 0.34, p = 0.04) and QOLIE-31 (r = -0.43, p = 0.007) suggested support for construct validity. Select items demonstrated low endorsement and weak association with the total score.
Findings provide preliminary support for the EComp as a tool for assessing compensatory strategy use in adults with epilepsy. Understanding these adaptive behaviors and functional needs can assist providers in formulating treatment plans and interventions. Future research with larger and diverse epilepsy samples will be necessary to confirm structural validity.

title: Sustained Viral Suppression and its association with Psychiatric Morbidity and Sleep Quality among Older Adults with Human Immunodeficiency Virus: Evidence from a Retrospective Cohort in Ibadan, Nigeria.
abstract:
Purpose Older adults with HIV are at risk of psychiatric disorders and poor sleep quality, but evidence from sub-Saharan Africa is limited, particularly regarding sustained viral suppression. This study examined the prevalence of psychiatric disorders and poor sleep quality symptoms and their association with sustained viral suppression among older adults with HIV in Nigeria.
A retrospective cohort study was conducted among older adults receiving care at a tertiary HIV clinic in Ibadan, Nigeria. Viral load data from 2019-2023 were abstracted from medical records to determine sustained viral load suppression, while psychiatric morbidity and sleep quality were assessed cross-sectionally in 2023. Psychiatric assessments included major depressive disorder, anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder and mania. Mixed-effects logistic regression assessed changes in viral suppression over time and associations with psychiatric morbidity and sleep quality.
Among 400 participants, 63.5% were female and mean age was 58.2 years (S.D 6.5). A total of 25.8% had major depressive disorder, 17.5% had anxiety disorder, 29.3% had poor sleep quality, 3.3%, bipolar disorder, and 1.0% mania. Viral suppression improved significantly over the retrospective period. Sustained viral suppression was significantly associated with higher odds of good sleep quality (OR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.07 to 2.66, p = 0.025), but not psychiatric morbidity.
Psychiatric disorders and poor sleep quality are common among older adults with HIV in Nigeria. Sustained viral suppression was associated with better sleep quality but not psychiatric morbidity highlighting the importance of integrating mental health and sleep assessment into comprehensive HIV care for older adults.

title: The spatial extent of fast ripples is associated with cognitive and language deficits in children with focal epilepsy: An exploratory SEEG study.
abstract:
To determine if the spatial extent of interictal fast ripples in focal epilepsy patients is associated with brain dysfunction.
Thirty pediatric focal epilepsy patients who underwent SEEG investigation had their cognitive and language deficits assessed in scales of 0 to 4. Fast ripples (250-500 Hz), ripples (80-250 Hz), and IEDs were automatically detected in 10 min during NREM sleep. We fitted linear models to the relationship between the cognitive deficit scale and the spatial spread of the interictal neurophysiologic events (number of channels with rate of events > 10 % of maximum rate). For the language deficit, we computed the Spearman correlation between the median rate of events in all brain regions and the deficit scale.
Cognitive deficit scale was significantly associated with the number of channels with fast ripples (p = 0.049), not so with ripples (p = 0.31), IEDs (p = 0.31). The potential confound of number of explored channels did not improve the fitting of the models. Language deficits were not correlated with the number of channels showing interictal events. However, from all brain regions the most statistically significant correlations (p < 0.01) were between median fast ripple rates in the left and right pars opercularis and triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area and its contralateral counterpart) with r = 0.66, p = 0.003 (18 patients), in the superior temporal gyrus in the language dominant hemisphere with r = 0.72, p = 0.005 (13 patients), and the dominant basal temporal region with r = 0.79, p = 0.006 (10 patients). Median rates of IEDs and ripples exhibited lower correlation with language deficits in these regions.
Widespread fast ripples are associated with increased cognitive deficits, and language deficiencies are correlated with fast ripple rates in brain regions associated with language. The extent of fast-ripple activity was associated with cognitive deficit severity in this cohort, whereas the corresponding associations for ripples and IEDs did not reach statistical significance.

title: Topography-specific white matter hyperintensities, hippocampal atrophy, and gait slowing as independent and interrelated correlates of late-life depression.
abstract:
Late-life depression (LLD) has been linked to cerebrovascular disease, neurodegeneration, and physical dysfunction. This study aimed to investigate the independent and interrelated associations of topography-specific white matter hyperintensities (WMH) burden, hippocampal volume, and gait speed with LLD.
We evaluated 366 older adults (LLD n = 112; non-depressed n = 254) using 3 T MRI, neuropsychological testing, and gait speed assessment. WMH were segmented into juxtaventricular (JVWMH), periventricular (PVWMH), and deep (DWMH) regions. Multivariable logistic and linear regressions and structural path analysis were performed.
JVWMH (OR = 2.98, 95% CI 1.58-5.63, p = 0.001) and PVWMH volume (OR = 2.60, 95% CI 1.61-4.18, p < 0.001), together with slower gait (OR = 0.96, 95% CI 0.95-0.98, p < 0.001) were associated with LLD, whereas DWMH was not. In linear models, JVWMH (β = 0.184, P = 0.001), PVWMH (β = 0.197, P < 0.001), smaller hippocampus volume (β = -0.115, p = 0.038), and slower gait (β = -0.322, p < 0.001) were independently associated with increased depressive symptom severity, whereas DWMH was not. Path analysis demonstrated that JVWMH exerted both direct (β = 0.17, p < 0.001) and indirect effects on depression via gait slowing (β = 0.044, p = 0.007), whereas PVWMH showed only direct effects and DWMH showed no significant pathways.
This study reveals that LLD is independently associated with regional WMH, hippocampal volume loss, and gait slowing, via topography-specific direct and indirect WMH pathways.

title: An Automated Framework Using Magnetic Resonance Imaging Feature Masking and Support Vector Machine for Schizophrenia Classification.
abstract: Automated classification of schizophrenia can improve the quality of life for people with schizophrenia and reduce social costs. At present, however, the usual standards for diagnosing mental illnesses are still based on the subjective assessment of psychiatrists and lack objective quantitative biomarkers for early detection. Neuroimaging-based machine learning has achieved some success, but the existing models have not addressed the high dimensionality of small-sample magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies. These data characteristics are prone to sub-optimal automatic feature extraction and weak out-of-sample generalization. Based on the above problems, an automated classification pipeline that combines MRI feature engineering with a support vector machine (SVM) classifier to accurately differentiate patients with schizophrenia is introduced. First, to address inter-subject anatomical differences, comprehensive brain preprocessing and spatial alignment were performed. Then, intensity-based statistical features were derived from the preprocessed volumes, reduced in the input space via background masking to remove non-brain tissues, and subsequently aggregated into atlas-based regional features. A refined feature matrix is then fed into an SVM to construct the optimal separating hyperplane for final classification. This study adopted an 80:20 train-test split strategy, with five-fold cross-validation performed exclusively on the training set for model selection and hyperparameter tuning, followed by final performance evaluation on the held-out test set. Using the public COBRE dataset, the final SVM model achieved an accuracy of 96.7% on the held-out test set. This framework is expected to evolve into an objective, data-driven auxiliary diagnostic tool for schizophrenia and to provide timely treatment decision support in clinical practice.

title: Developing an Empirically Derived Head Trauma Burden Assessment Score for Intimate Partner Violence-related Neurotrauma.
abstract:
To develop a statistically derived and clinically informed intimate partner violence-related head trauma (IPV-HT) Burden Assessment Score that accounts for diverse brain injury mechanisms (eg, nonfatal strangulation, blunt force), exposure chronicity, and injury severity.
Community-based sample.
Females (N = 146; 38.7 ± 10.2 years old, 56.8% White/Non-Hispanic) reporting at least 1 IPV-HT on the Brain Injury Screening Questionnaire IPV module (BISQ-IPV).
Cross-sectional analysis.
Candidate variables representing injury mechanism, frequency, severity, and IPV relationship history were extracted from the BISQ-IPV. Multicollinearity screening and multivariable linear regression selected variables predicting Rivermead Postconcussion Symptoms Questionnaire (RPQ) total scores. Leave-one-out elimination identified the most predictive variables determined by change in R2 when removed. Retained variables were standardized and combined to calculate the IPV-HT Burden Assessment Score, normalized to range 1-100 (low-to-high burden). Scores were correlated with Adverse Childhood Experiences questionnaire (ACEs), Headache Impact Test (HIT-6), cognition subscale of the Quality of Life in Neurological Disorders (NeuroQoL), Post-traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5), Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-Q-IV), and Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D).
Five variables were retained in the final model, achieving 25% explainability of RPQ total scores (R2 = 0.25; adjusted R2 = 0.22). Count of unique IPV-related brain injury mechanisms explained most RPQ variance (∼19%), followed by number of IPV relationships, and duration of the 3 most severe relationships. The model also retained the proportion of injuries due to nonfatal strangulation meeting brain injury criteria and the average brain injury severity. The final IPV-HT Burden Assessment Score (mean = 31.7 ± 18.24, range = 2-86) positively correlated with ACEs (r = 0.17, P = 0.043), HIT-6 (r = 0.27, P = 0.001), PCL-5 (r = 0.23, P = 0.006), GAD-Q-IV (r = 0.17, P = 0.043), and CES-D (r = 0.29, P < 0.001) and negatively correlated with NeuroQoL T-scores (r = -0.30, P < 0.001).
The IPV-HT Burden Assessment Score captures diverse IPV-HT exposures and shows preliminary validity through associations with psychosocial and neurological outcomes.

title: Gray matter volume alterations in generalized anxiety disorder and major depressive disorder.
abstract:
Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and major depressive disorder (MDD) are highly comorbid and clinically overlapping, but their shared and differential structural brain alterations remain unclear. This study investigated gray matter volume (GMV) alterations in GAD and MDD using voxel-based morphometry (VBM).
A total of 168 right-handed participants, including 42 patients with GAD, 43 patients with MDD, and 83 healthy controls (HCs), underwent high-resolution T1-weighted MRI. Whole-brain VBM analyses were performed to compare GMV differences among the three groups, controlling for age, sex, education, and total intracranial volume. Post hoc analyses were conducted for significant clusters, and partial correlation analyses examined associations between abnormal GMV and symptom severity.
Significant group differences in GMV were found in the left middle frontal gyrus, left postcentral gyrus, left putamen, and right superior frontal gyrus. Both GAD and MDD patients showed decreased GMV in the left middle frontal gyrus and left postcentral gyrus, and increased GMV in the left putamen, compared with HCs. In contrast, decreased GMV in the right superior frontal gyrus was observed only in MDD patients and was positively correlated with both anxiety and depressive symptom severity.
These findings suggest that GAD and MDD share GMV alterations in prefrontal, somatosensory, and striatal regions, whereas reduced GMV in the right superior frontal gyrus was observed only in the MDD group.

title: Comparative Hippocampal and Serum Metabolomics Reveals Dose-related Metabolic Alterations Consistent with TDMQ20 Intervention in a Cu-Aβ₄₂-induced Mouse Model.
abstract: Copper (Cu) dyshomeostasis and metabolic dysfunction have been implicated as key drivers of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Tetradentate monoquinoline 20 (TDMQ20), a Cu chelator, reportedly improves behavioral deficits in AD model mice, but its underlying metabolic mechanism is unclear. Here, we addressed this via untargeted ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS) metabolomics in the hippocampus and serum of AD model mice induced by intrahippocampal injection of Cu amyloid-β42 (Cu-Aβ₄₂) and then treated with TDMQ20 at low (LT, 5 mg/kg) and high (HT, 10 mg/kg) doses. Results showed that AD was associated with tissue-specific metabolic perturbations: hippocampal disorders were enriched in linoleic acid and glycerophospholipid metabolism, while serum perturbations centered on tryptophan, sphingolipid, and purine metabolism, with organic acids, lipids, and benzenoids as core differential metabolite classes. TDMQ20 reversed these abnormalities in a dose-associated manner: LT regulated tryptophan/linoleic acid metabolism in the hippocampus and purine/arachidonic acid metabolism in serum, while HT shifted the hippocampal metabolic profile substantially toward that of the control group. Cross-matrix analysis identified PS (15:0/22:0) and LPC (18:2/0:0) as key lipid metabolites with opposite expression patterns between hippocampus and serum, and four serum endogenous metabolites (pipecolic acid, PGG2, N-sulfo-D-glucosamine, and hex-2-ulose) as exploratory candidate metabolites. TDMQ20 was associated with metabolomic changes in both hippocampus and serum consistent with attenuated oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and membrane lipid remodeling, suggesting preferential central metabolic modulation and dose-associated action. This study provides metabolomic evidence consistent with TDMQ20's potential tissue-resolved regulatory properties and identifies exploratory candidate metabolites for monitoring therapeutic efficacy in AD.

title: Independent Validation of the volBrain CognitiveTree Automated MRI Pipeline in Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis.
abstract: In Alzheimer's disease, significant structural changes are observed in various brain regions, particularly in the cerebral cortex. The aim of this study is to contribute to the diagnosis of the disease by conducting comparative analyses between Alzheimer's patients and a healthy control group. Magnetic resonance images from Alzheimer's disease and healthy control groups, comprising 100 individuals in each group, were retrospectively obtained from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. Image analysis was performed using the CognitiveTree module within the volBrain software. In this context, percentage values for the right, left, and total volumes of 231 distinct anatomical regions of the brain were analyzed using various statistical methods. In the classification analysis of Alzheimer's disease and healthy control groups, the highest accuracy rate of 90% was achieved using the Random Forest and Bagging Classifier models. The parameter with the greatest impact on the classification analysis was the total volume of the inferior lateral ventricle. In the machine learning analysis conducted using a 20% test set, the highest AUC value of 0.95 was obtained with the Random Forest algorithm. A higher AUC value was observed compared to the Bagging model; however, the DeLong test determined that this difference was not statistically significant (p > 0.05). Findings from the classification analysis of Alzheimer's disease and healthy control groups indicate that machine learning-based models offer an effective approach for the rapid and practical prediction of the disease. It is anticipated that the integration of these methods into clinical practice, along with an evaluation of their applicability across different populations, could contribute to diagnostic processes.

title: Validation of the Russian version of the cognitive functioning self‑assessment scale (CFSS) in patients with non‑psychotic mental disorders.
abstract:
Cognitive assessment is vital for detecting impairments affecting quality of life, occupational functioning, and prognosis. While objective cognitive tests are available, tools assessing subjective cognition are limited. This study aimed to translate and culturally adapt the Cognitive Functioning Self-Assessment Scale (CFSS) into Russian and to examine its internal consistency, structural validity, and convergent validity in patients with non-psychotic mental disorders.
The CFSS was translated and culturally adapted into Russian following international guidelines. The sample consisted of 322 consecutively recruited patients (18-60 years) with non-psychotic mental disorders. Participants completed the Russian version of CFSS, Patient Health Questionnaire‑9 (PHQ‑9), Generalized Anxiety Disorder‑7 (GAD‑7), and the cognitive facet of the World Health Organization Quality of Life instrument (WHOQOL‑100).
The Russian version of CFSS showed excellent internal consistency (α = 0.925; ω = 0.929). ESEM supported a one‑factor structure with acceptable fit (CFI = 0.985; TLI = 0.983; RMSEA = 0.072). CFSS scores were associated with the WHOQOL‑100 cognitive facet (r = -0.67, p < 0.001), PHQ‑9 (r = 0.55, p < 0.001), and GAD‑7 (r = 0.36, p < 0.001). In an exploratory secondary analysis, participants with higher CFSS scores differed from those with lower CFSS scores in several sociodemographic and self-reported clinical characteristics.
The Russian version of CFSS is a reliable, valid, and practical instrument for assessing subjective cognitive functioning in patients with non‑psychotic psychiatric disorders. Further studies incorporating objective neuropsychological measures and repeated assessments are needed to evaluate concurrent/criterion-related validity and temporal reliability.

title: ClC-7 links PIKfyve inhibition to Rab-dependent LRRK2 activity at lysosomes.
abstract: Increased activity of leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) confers Parkinson's disease risk. LRRK2 dynamically localizes to lysosomal membranes in response to various stresses, yet the mechanisms by which distinct lysosomal perturbations are communicated to LRRK2 remain unclear. Here, we show that inhibition of the lysosomal lipid kinase PIKfyve promotes LRRK2 recruitment and signaling through a pathway that requires the lysosomal chloride/proton antiporter ClC-7. ClC-7 in turn controls the accumulation of multiple Rab GTPases on lysosomes. LRRK2 signaling under these conditions requires its established Rab-binding surfaces, with Rab12 contributing significantly to this response. This pathway operates independently of CASM. In contrast, lysosomal stresses that induce CASM require both Rab-binding sites on LRRK2 and GABARAP for robust LRRK2 signaling. These findings identify ClC-7-dependent lysosomal remodeling and Rab accumulation as key features linking PIKfyve inhibition to LRRK2 signaling and reveal that distinct lysosomal stresses engage different combinations of Rab and GABARAP inputs to activate LRRK2.

title: Cerebrospinal fluid and dural accumulation of α-synuclein impairs CNS clearance in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the build-up of α-synuclein (α-syn) in the brain, where it drives neurodegeneration. Importantly, aggregated α-syn also accumulates in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of PD patients, and while increasingly used for diagnosis, its pathological role remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that α-syn accumulation in central nervous system (CNS) border tissues promotes CNS clearance deficits, as observed in PD patients. We find that aggregated α-syn accumulates not only in the CSF but also in the dura mater of individuals with PD, and, using acute and chronic mouse models, show that α-syn deposition in these sites induces immune alterations in CNS borders and disrupts CNS clearance. Mechanistically, we reveal that α-syn at CNS borders elevates CSF TNF and demonstrate that both TNF and α-syn aggregates themselves impair lymphatic endothelial cell function. These findings demonstrate a pathological role for α-syn in the CNS border tissues and position meningeal immunity as a contributor to CNS clearance deficits in PD pathogenesis.

title: The whistle-smile reflex in Parkinson's disease: an exploratory case-control study.
abstract:
Parkinson's disease (PD) is a well-known neurodegenerative disease characterized by tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia. In 1943, Frederic Hanes described the whistle-smile reflex (WSR), noting its absence in PD patients due to reduced facial movements.
To assess the WSR's diagnostic performance.
In the current cross-sectional study, we selected PD patients and healthy controls. They were filmed while asked to whistle, and a blinded physician assessed if the individuals smiled or not. Absence of smiling after whistling was considered a positive test. We stratified the smiling intensity into 4 groups. We calculated the odds ratio (OR) of the positive WSR in PD and asymptomatic patients, which was reported with CIs, sensitivity (SE), specificity (SP), positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and we plotted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.
We identified 43 patients with PD (mean age = 63 ± 10 years; 30% of female subjects) and 44 asymptomatic controls (mean age = 64 ± 10 years; 51% of female subjects). The WSR test was positive in 35/43 PD cases versus 7/44 in the asymptomatic group (OR = 23.1; 95%CI = 7.6-70.5; SE = 81.4%; SP = 84.1%; PPV = 83.3%; NPV = 82.2%). When stratified considering the group with the least intense smile as a positive test, the test was positive in 42/43 PD cases versus 23/44 in the asymptomatic group (OR = 38.3; 95%CI = 4.8-303.7; SE = 97.7%; SP = 47.7%; PPV = 64.6%; NPV = 95.4%).
The WSR test showed a good performance in identifying PD patients; it may complement the physical examination, and its result may be a useful finding during the assessment of a patient with PD.
